**“under it in the shadow, till”** — in the manner of Scripture it ascribes human feelings to God
4.6:
**“And he prepared”** — In the Hebrew, ciceion is read for “gourd,” which springs up quickly and quickly withers. It is compared to Israel, putting down small roots into the earth and striving to lift itself on high, but not equalling the height of God’s cedars or firs.
**“And the Lord God prepared an ivy”** — A gourd or ivy: a kind of shrub or small tree with broad leaves, giving very thick shade, which creeps along the ground and does not reach higher without props to lean on. But God prepared this one so that, rising suddenly on high without any supports, it might give the prophet a shelter; and in this the power of God was shown. To this ivy or gourd is compared Israel, which once sheltered Jonah under its shade, Jonah awaiting in Christ the conversion of the Gentiles; and it gave him no small joy, making him a shelter rather than a house, having the look of a roof but no foundations.
**“and it came up”** — suddenly, by God’s wonderful power
4.7:
**“And he prepared”** — Some understand the worm and the burning wind as the Romans, who destroyed Israel after the resurrection of Christ.
**“a worm”** — Christ, who says, “I am a worm, and no man.”
**“when the morning arose on the following day: and it struck the ivy”** — which flourished before the Sun of righteousness rose; but when Christ rose, the shelter was left without God’s help and lost all its green
4.8:
**“And when the sun was risen”** — by whose light the darkness of the Ninevites was scattered
**“the Lord commanded a hot”** — Hence in Hosea: “The Lord will bring a burning wind that shall rise from the desert, and it shall dry up his springs, and shall make his fountains desolate.”
**“and burning wind: and the sun beat upon the head of Jonas, and he broiled with the heat”** — with Israel
**“and he desired for his soul that he might die”** — In baptism, as in a bath, that he may receive back the moisture he had lost by denying. Hence Peter says to the parched Jews: “Do penance, and be baptized every one of you, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.”
4.9:
**“And the Lord said”** — the Father
**“to Jonas”** — the Son
**“Dost thou think thou hast reason”** — Above, when the Ninevites repented and were saved, the prophet, asked the same, answered nothing, but approved God’s question by his silence; for, knowing God to be merciful and forgiving of evils, he did not grieve at the salvation of the Gentiles. But here, because the gourd has dried up and Israel withers, and he is asked pointedly, “Dost thou think thou hast reason to be angry, for the ivy?”, he says boldly: “I have reason to be sorrowful, even unto death; for I did not wish to save others in such a way that others perished, nor to win strangers in such a way that I lost my own.” So Christ mourns for Jerusalem even unto death, not his own death but the Jews’, that they may die denying and rise confessing the Son of God.
4.10:
**“And the Lord said: Thou”** — Son
**“art grieved for the ivy”** — for the Jews condemned
**“thou hast not laboured”** — As regards the people of the Gentiles. Hence Israel says plainly: “Behold, for so many years do I serve thee, and thou hast never given me a kid; but for this one, who hath devoured his substance with harlots, thou hast killed the fatted calf.” He is not refuted in this, but hears: “All I have is thine.” Yet it was meet to make merry for the brother’s return. For it was for the Gentiles that Christ’s precious blood was shed, and he went down to hell that that people might go up to heaven. No such toil was spent for the sons of Israel; and so he envies the younger brother.
**“in one night”** — that is, the time before the coming of Christ
**“came up, and in one night perished”** — when the Sun of righteousness set for it
4.11:
**“And shall not I spare Ninive, that great city”** — by which is signified the Church, in which the number is greater than the twelve tribes of Israel
**“in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand persons that know not how to distinguish between their right hand and their left, and many beasts?”** — a great number of creatures without reason
**“more than a hundred and twenty”** — This can be understood of the age of infants, which is innocent and simple; and since the number of little ones is so great, it is plain that the multitude of older age was great. Or, since Nineveh is a great city, and in a great house there are vessels not only of gold but also of earthenware, it can be said that there was a great multitude which, before it did penance, did not know the difference between good and evil.

1.1:
**“The word”**
• that is,
• that which “was in the beginning with God”
**“of the Lord”** — the Father

1.6:
**“Who can stand before the face of his indignation? and who shall resist in the fierceness of his anger?”** — no one, because:
**“Before the face”** — When the Lord comes in the whirlwind, drying up the sea, that is, the empire of the Assyrians, and destroying all the rivers, that is, their power and plenty, and shaking the mountains, that is, the height of the empire, and its breadth, which is called the world, then no power will be able to resist God when he is angry and avenging his people.
**“in the fierceness of his anger”** — By the wrath is signified the devil, the minister of wrath, who will be sent to punish the wicked; nor will anyone be found at the end of the world so pure as to resist him with a free brow, saying: Behold, “the prince of this world cometh, and in me he hath not any thing.”
**“his indignation is poured out”** — or: has dropped
**“like fire: and the rocks are melted by him”**
• when God rebukes, few or none will there be who do not tremble at the judgement of God, since even “the stars are not pure in his sight”
• The indignation of God, which long bears with sinners, sometimes does not break out wholly in punishment, but drops like fire, to dissolve the hardness of hearts, which is signified by the rock.
1.7:
**“The Lord is good”**
• to his own
• When he begins to be angry with the nations and to lay waste their kingdoms, then he will not overwhelm his own who are sailing with the same storm.
**“and giveth strength in the day of trouble”** — of captivity, or of judgement
**“and knoweth them that hope in him”** — He will not overwhelm his own with the Assyrians, because in patience they wait for his coming. For “the Lord knoweth who are his.”
1.8:
**“But with a flood that passeth by”** — not abiding, because
**“an utter end”** — that is, an end
**“he will make … of the place thereof”** — that is, of the flood; as it is said: “I passed by, and lo, he was not … his place was not found,” and: “the way of the wicked shall perish”; so the way of the flood will perish, and after the wrath of God only his clemency will appear
**“and his enemies”** — who have chosen darkness rather than light will be seized by the darkness itself.
**“But with a flood”** — According to the history: when God has laid waste the land of promise as if by a flood, he will make an end of the captivity, bringing Israel back to its former seats; but darkness will pursue the Assyrians. The same can be said of the end of the world: that after his wrath he will have mercy on the saints, and will send the persecutors, or the devils, into the exterior darkness.
1.9:
**“What do ye devise against the Lord? he will make an utter end”**
• or: it will be made
• he who created the world will himself make its end
**“What do ye devise against”** — Since God is to make an end of the flood for his faithful, why do you accuse the God of the law, as if, too severe and stern, he inflicted heavy torments on sinners by the command of the law? If he seems bloody because he destroyed the human race by the flood, the Sodomites by fire, the Egyptians by the sea, the Israelites in the wilderness, know that he punished them in time for their sins so that he might not punish them for ever, because “God will not judge twice for the same thing.” Those, then, who have been sufficiently punished will not be punished afterwards; otherwise Scripture lies, which it is wicked to say.
**“there shall not rise a double affliction”**
• If one of the faithful, caught in adultery, is beheaded, it seems that he is not to be punished further, “lest he be judged twice for the same thing.” But it must be known that “God, as he knows the measure of all things, so knows also the measure of punishments; and the sentence of the judge is not forestalled, nor is the power taken from him of exercising punishment on the sinner hereafter; and a great sin is atoned for by long torments, but a light fault is paid for by a light punishment.”
• The Hebrews' explanation: O Assyrians, why do you think evil against God, that he will destroy the twelve tribes entirely? There shall not rise a double affliction: he will not hand over Juda and Jerusalem to you as he handed over the ten tribes and Samaria.
1.10:
**“For as thorns embrace one another: so while they are feasting and drinking together, they shall be consumed as stubble that is fully dry”**
• The two tribes will not be taken by the Assyrians as the ten were, because, while the Assyrians are still in the land of Juda, and embrace one another like thorns, rejoicing and glad, they will be consumed by the angel, when in one night a hundred and eighty-five thousand were slain; a multitude well compared to a feast of drunkards, and to thorns embracing one another, which are wont to be given to the fire, and to stubble, which is burnt up by a light flame.
• The covenants and alliances of the heretics embrace one another like thorns; and their feast, that is, the mysteries of the altar (for they too say that they have the Lord's table), is a covenant of thorns, eating together and drinking alike. For when, drunk on the vineyard of Sodom, they blaspheme against God, is it not a feast of thorns? Yet it will be consumed with its authors like stubble that is fully dry, since from them goes out the hostile thought against God.
1.11:
**“Out of thee shall come forth one that imagineth evil against the Lord”** — heresies, zealously
**“contriving treachery in his mind”** — so as to carry on the lie with inventions
**“Out of thee”** — This is said of Rabsaces, who went out from the Assyrians and blasphemed God, persuading the Israelites to despair of God's help and give themselves up to the Assyrians, to serve not God but idols.
1.12:
**“Thus saith the Lord: Though they were perfect”**
• in strength
• As if to say: though the Assyrians are strong and many, they will not prevail against you.
**“they were”** — the Assyrians
**“and many of them so”** — having joined many nations to themselves
**“yet thus shall they be cut off”**
• the angel laying waste
• that is, the Assyrians
• As many hairs by the shears, so their multitude will easily be cut down.
**“and he shall pass”** — Assur will either cease to be, or, his army laid waste, will return to his own country, leaving you safe
**“Though they were perfect”**
• Again the word is directed to Juda and Jerusalem, to whom God promises security, not for ever, but for that time and from those enemies by whom they were besieged.
• God's kindly threat against the heretics: though they are strong and many, they will be worn down, and their onset will pass. There follows also a promise: I have let you be afflicted by the power of the devil, at whose prompting you had invented so much and had woven bonds to bind the souls of sinners; but all these I will now break, saying to those who were held in bonds: Come out.
1.13:
**“And now I will break in pieces his rod”**
• the power
• with which he tried to strike you
**“his”** — of the Assyrian
**“with which he struck thy back, and I will burst thy bonds asunder”** — which the captor was preparing; although the siege can also be taken for the bonds of the shut-in multitude
1.14:
**“And the Lord will give a commandment concerning thee”**
• against you, Assur
• having made the promise of deliverance to the Israelites, he turns his words to the Assyrians, threatening them with punishment.
**“that no more … shall be sown”** — that is, there will be no sowing
**“of thy name”** — because Sennacherib, having returned to Ninive, was at once killed by his sons in the house of his god while worshipping; punished there whence he hoped for help
**“I will destroy … out of the house of thy God”** — you
**“the graven and molten thing … I will make it thy grave”** — among the altars and couches of the one worshipping idols, wicked blood will be shed.
**“for thou art disgraced”**
• And the Lord will give a commandment concerning thee. O Assur, what you are to suffer, do not think it happens by chance and without a judge, because all things will be done at God's command.
• O heretic, the souls deceived by you will not take up the names they had called upon over their lands before, but the sects of the heretics will cease, so that others are not named after them. So the doctrines of errors will die to you; and you too, who seemed to yourself to live, will die to error, and, dead to your own good, you will have the idols you worshipped as your grave; and errors will be taken from your breast, in which before was the temple of your God, whom you feigned. Because you are disgraced, while you worship vain idols, you who are rational.
1.15:
**“Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, and that preacheth peace: O Juda, keep thy festivals, and pay thy vows”** — singing to the Lord with the angels
**“for Belial shall no more pass through thee again”**
• the transgressor
• Hence the Apostle: “What concord hath Christ with Belial?”
**“he is utterly cut off”**
• because
• Ninive being overthrown
• Behold upon the mountains. We read in Paralipomenon that, while Sennacherib was besieging Jerusalem, the pasch could not be kept in the first month; but when his army had been slain and the death of Sennacherib announced, the pasch was celebrated in the second month. Hence he says: O Juda, do not be anxious; your enemy has been killed in the temple of his god; behold, a messenger comes to you running over the mountains and hills, and, as if from a watchtower, announces to you that by Sennacherib's death the city is set free. Keep, then, your festivals, and pay to God the vows you promised, for the death of the enemy; because Belial, that is, that transgressor, will not pass through you, for he has wholly perished: the army and the king and the empire of the Assyrians have utterly fallen.
• If at any time there has been a heavy persecution, and God's vengeance has appeared on its adversaries, let us say to the Church: O Juda, keep thy festivals, and pay thy vows.
• Allegorically. The heresies destroyed, the voice of the Church's preacher is brought in, urging to joy the souls that confess God, for the devil destroyed in the idols and with the idols.

2.1:
**“He is come up that”** — Having announced the destruction of Ninive, he adds by whom it is to be carried out, directing his words to Ninive herself.
**“He is come up that shall destroy before thy face”** — Nabuchodonosor, who will besiege you, lay waste the fields before your face, hunt down the farmers, and hold you shut in.
**“that shall keep the siege: watch the way”** — O Ninive, the things I foretell will come upon you
**“watch”** — The prophet, seeing war hanging over Ninive, already mocks her with joy as she is about to fall.
**“fortify”** — gird yourself
**“thy loins”** — mockery
**“strengthen thy power exceedingly”**
• gather armies
• Allegorically. Three things are commanded to Juda: first, that he look to the way by which he may walk to him who says: “I am the way”; then, that he hold his loins, that is, mortify the flesh; third, that he take up power, so as not to fail in the war against the enemies. And so that he may not fail in this war, he adds in what he can have hope: namely, that God has rendered the pride of Jacob; the wrongs which in his pride he used to do to others he now, humbled by God's grace, bears patiently from the Assyrians. Jacob means “supplanter,” Israel “seeing God.” As, then, seeing God and always thinking of God, he does not know how to do wrong to others, so, supplanting his enemies in the wrestling, he ceases to do wrong to others, because the spoilers, that is, the angels of each one, “who see the face of the Father,” have scattered in Jacob and Israel whatever dust had clung to them, and have turned away from the true Jacob and Israel the mind that before was quick to insult, and have put out whatever evil was spreading in their thoughts.
2.2:
**“For the Lord hath rendered”** — as God avenged Juda on the pride of Sennacherib, so he avenged the ten tribes, who will be held by Ninive
**“the pride of Jacob”** — which he used against Juda
**“as the pride of Israel: because the spoilers”** — the Assyrians
**“have laid them waste”** — Juda and Israel
**“because the spoilers”** — According to the history, he speaks against Ninive, and the army of the Babylonians coming against her is described.
**“and … vine branches”** — metaphorically
**“their”** — of Juda and Israel
**“have marred”**
• For … hath rendered. The Septuagint: For the Lord hath turned away the captivity of Jacob, as the insult of Israel.
• The Assyrians laid waste both Juda and Israel.
2.3:
**“The shield of his mighty men is like fire”**
• because the Ninivites laid waste Israel, therefore the shield, that is, the strength of the Babylonians, will blaze against Ninive
• Allegorically. The shield, that is, the arms of the devil and his members, are kindled with the fire of envy, of anger and fury; and the men of his army are red in scarlet with the blood of the martyrs. The flaming reins of the chariot that carries the devil through the world are set on fire with the fire of hell; the drivers, who hunt prey for the devil, are stupefied and take their pleasure, and as it were sleep when the prey is taken. But all these, for their evil ways, will be thrown into confusion in the day of judgement, and the chariots are jostled in the streets. Though broad is the way that leads to death, yet, in the pressure of the shortened time, they will not be able to find the right road, but will dash against one another; yet there they will breathe their old fury, and run to and fro like lightning. And the devil and his members will remember, to their own punishment, those who acted mightily and violently against the Church; and they will stumble in their ways, unable to carry out their attempts, and will swiftly go up on her walls. Weakened by terror at the coming judge, they will flee to the ends of the world, by which, as by walls, the world is shut in and surrounded; and, unable to go further, they will be forced as if by necessity to fight against him who presses on them. But while they think this, all that they had gained will be scattered, and the gates that had been shut will be opened, that is, the consciences of each will be revealed; and the kingdoms of the wicked will fall, and the soldier, the devil, and his bondwomen, that is, the soft who are under him, will be led into Tartarus, groaning and indignant against themselves for the evils they have done, and yet murmuring and indignant against God for the punishments they suffer; for they would not have God as their punisher.
**“the men of the army are clad in scarlet”** — ready for the shedding of blood
**“are flaming”** — were
**“the reins … are flaming”** — In the burning reins is signified the swiftness of those hastening, and the pomp of those preparing for war is told; and the Scripture is woven together, mixing now what Israel once suffered, now what the Assyrian did, now what the Babylonians carry out against the Assyrians.
**“the reins of the chariot … in the day”** — elsewhere: in the day
**“of his preparation, and the drivers are stupefied”** — No wonder the Babylonians come so swiftly to lay waste, since the Israelites, or the Ninivites, once the drivers of others, were now useless.
2.4:
**“They are in confusion in the ways”** — they are mingled together
**“the chariots jostle one against another in the streets”** — dashed against one another
**“their looks”**
• of the Babylonians
• namely, so that they may terrify with their face the enemy before they strike him with the sword
**“in the ways”** — Again he returns to the order of the description: so great is the multitude of those coming that the column on the road is mixed and cannot be told apart. The chariots too, for the multitude, will dash against one another in the streets.
2.5:
**“He will muster up”** — he will look for those who fell in the flight
**“his valiant men”** — before
**“they shall stumble in their march: they shall quickly get upon the walls thereof”** — Not withstanding the force of the enemy, they will enter the walls of Ninive
**“and a covering shall be prepared”** — because of the long siege, to keep off the heat, the enemy will make shelters
2.6: **“The gates of the rivers”** — Though the Ninivites shut the gates, the Lord unbars them, and they are opened to the Babylonians; the gates held a multitude of citizens like a river; and the temple, that is, the kingdom, is destroyed.
2.7:
**“And the soldier is led away captive”** — all were led to Babylon
**“and her bondwomen”**
• the lesser towns and strongholds
• captive women
• Under the figure of a woman taken captive the laying waste of Ninive is described.
**“were led away”** — by the victors
**“mourning as doves, murmuring in their hearts”** — So great will be the terror that not even a sob will break out, but, like softly cooing doves, they will swallow their tears with a dim murmur
2.8:
**“And as for Ninive”**
• the world
• When the daughters, that is, the lesser towns, have been destroyed, the people of Ninive itself, which for its multitude is compared to pools of water, will be so useless that, unable to resist the enemy, it will flee.
**“Stand, stand”** — To the peoples fleeing with their goods Ninive cries out like a mother: Stand, stand; shut the gates; at least resist the enemy on the walls. But no one turns back out of love for his mother; they abandon her as prey to the enemy. Hence the voice is directed to the Babylonians: Take the spoil of the gold.
**“but there is none that will return back”**
• to the mother who cries out
• Allegorically. The waters of Ninive, that is, of the world, are those who, leaving the height of heaven, have slipped to the depths; for all the teachings of the world which are outside the garden enclosed, though they seem great, are yet confined within a narrow bound.
• Allegorically. The first thing is that the dwellers in the world should not flee from God by sinning; but if they have fled, at the voice of God, or of mother Church calling them back and saying, You have sinned, be still, one ought to cease from the flight, that is, from the fault; but the obstinate man will not return. To him it is said by the devil: Take with you the silver of worldly eloquence and the gold of worldly wisdom; adorn your teachings with the flower of every meaning and word. But the vessels, that is, their hearts, are so deep in desire that no multitude of riches, however great, can fill them.
2.9:
**“Take ye the spoil”**
• O Babylonians
• because the Ninivites have fled
**“of the silver, take the spoil of the gold”** — seize suddenly what was gathered over so long a time
**“for there is no end of the riches of all the precious furniture”** — you cannot seize as much as she offers to be seized
2.10:
**“She is destroyed”**
• Ninive
• This is of those who are converted to God, who, frozen before by unbelief, are scattered by the warmth of faith; and they rend their hearts by confessing, and tear them by repenting; and the heart, hard before, melts with the warmth of the Holy Spirit; and the knees, stiff before, are bent to God; and all the pleasures of the flesh fail. But what follows, and the faces of them all are as the blackness of a kettle, belongs to those who will not return, whose faces will be covered with confusion like a sooty pot.
**“and rent, and torn: the heart”** — her
**“melteth, and … fail”** — and in her is
**“the knees … and … lose their strength”** — the breaking
**“all the loins … and the faces of them all are as the blackness of a kettle”** — from the greatness of their fear the faces of the inhabitants will look like pots, burnt and disfigured
2.11:
**“Where is now the dwelling”**
• the dwelling
• Allegorically. When Ninive, that is, the world, has passed away, then the saints, wondering and rejoicing, will say: Where is the dwelling of the lions, to which went the devil, and also the whelp, that is, Antichrist, and every word of perverse teaching, which before the coming of Christ no one frightened away? But it killed very many by its demons, and filled its caves, that is, its churches, with corpses and the blood of the dead.
**“of the lions, and the feeding place of the young lions?”** — O Ninive, you were the dwelling of kings and the refreshment of nobles; but now you are no more, because the king of Babylon has invaded you.
**“to which”** — to storm it
**“the lion went”** — Nabuchodonosor
**“to”** — with none resisting
**“enter in thither, the young lion”** — his under-kings
2.12: **“The lion caught enough”** — Nabuchodonosor by right of victory possesses all things, and handed over the captives into servitude to his cities or his wives, and filled his treasuries and his cities with the plunder and the ornaments of Ninive.
2.13:
**“Behold I come against thee”**
• no other
• O Ninive, you will suffer all that has been said, by my doing
• Behold I come against thee: I send the Babylonians.
• Allegorically. God threatens the world that he will burn up the multitude that goes by the broad way to death, and stifle it with the smoke of its malice; and in his goodness the sword, that is, the word of God, will devour even the lions, so that from then on no one is taken to death by them; and he will put down all the din of evil works, which used to announce death to men.
**“saith the Lord”** — for whom to say is to do
**“of hosts, and I will burn … even to smoke”** — to the end
**“thy chariots”** — chariots
**“and … thy young lions”** — I will kill the nobles and under-kings with the sword
**“the sword shall devour: and I will cut off thy prey out of the land”** — you will no longer lay waste the land or exact tribute
**“and the voice of thy messengers shall be heard no more”**
• nor will your emissaries be heard through the provinces; or: I will not hear the angels who are set over you, praying for you.
• Allegorically, all these things can be understood of the confusion to come of those who are to be damned.

3.1:
**“Woe”** — to thee
**“O city of blood, all full of lies and violence”** — in which there is no truth but all lies; you, I say, full of rapine and the tearing of prey
**“Woe to thee, O city”**
• The power of Ninive is described, and under a lament her cruelty is rebuked.
• Allegorically. The world, which “is seated in wickedness” and kills men with its tongues, is called the city of blood; it is lying in the perversity of the teachings by which it tears and carries off many. In the world too is the noise of the whip, that is, of the tribulations under which the just cry out when they are afflicted: when one is tormented by anger, another by lust, another by hatred or envy, the whip of the Assyrian king sounds in them. Sometimes the devil's whip is felt in bodily diseases; for sometimes, not from the nature of the elements but from the devil striking, jaundice is sent, or dropsy, or the pain of the stone, and the like. In the world there is also the rattling of the wheel, when men, not knowing where safety is and where danger, run to and fro. There is also the neighing horse, that is, the devil, who fiercely pursues those who flee, tramples them and mocks them. There is also the running chariot, which is drowned with Pharao; it is drawn by four horses, that is, by the four passions of the mind. Hence: “Hence they desire and fear, grieve and rejoice.” In Ninive there sounds also the horseman coming up, that is, the devil, whose sword shines with the art of dialectic and rhetoric, and his spear glitters while he “transformeth himself into an angel of light”; and by these arms many are killed; and unless they are at once healed by grace, there is a grievous destruction, in which there is no end, because malice has no end. These evils fall, that is, they befall, on the bodies of the dead, which are laid low by the multiplying of fornication. And in Ninive there is a harlot, beautiful and agreeable, who draws almost everyone to love of her by various witchcrafts. She sells the nations in fornications, namely when, through love of temporal things and weariness of good things, those who had been members of Christ become “the members of an harlot,” and draw others with them.
3.2:
**“The noise of the whip”**
• of a savage empire
• O Ninive, is in you
• The army of Ninive preparing for war is described.
**“and the noise”** — the sound
**“of the rattling of the wheels”** — running about in all directions
**“and”** — the noise
**“of the neighing horse, and of the running chariot, and of the horsemen coming up”** — As many as are the kinds of sins, so many are the nations of Ninive.
3.3:
**“And of the shining sword, and”** — the noise
**“of the glittering spear, and of a multitude slain”** — the noise of the adversaries slain by the Ninivites
**“and”** — the noise
**“of a grievous destruction: and there is no end of carcasses, and they shall fall down on their dead bodies”** — either they will fall in their own multitude while they are crowded against one another, or they will fall over the corpses of the slain
**“and they shall fall down”** — The wanton both perish in soul and are weakened even now in the body they serve.
3.4:
**“Because of”** — see the cause
**“the multitude of the fornications of the harlot that was beautiful and agreeable”** — because she committed fornication with many nations, and worshipped the idols of the whole world which she had made subject to herself
**“and that made use of witchcraft”** — it signifies magicians
**“that sold nations through her fornications, and families through her witchcrafts”** — that is, she had power over all nations
3.5:
**“Behold”**
• I will come
• O Ninive, because you have made yourself ready for all fornications like a public brothel
**“I come against thee”** — to overthrow you
**“saith the Lord of hosts: and I will discover thy shame”** — I will not entrust your judgement to angels or to anyone else, but I myself will uncover your shame
**“to thy face”** — so that what you did not see before may be set before your eyes
**“and will shew thy nakedness to the nations, and thy shame to kingdoms”** — so that those who committed fornication with you may themselves despise you and mock you and heap insults on you, as an example to others, with all looking on
**“Behold I come against thee”** — He speaks under the figure of an adulterous woman who, caught, is brought out into the midst and stripped of her finery before the eyes of all.
3.6: **“And I will cast abominations upon thee, and will disgrace thee, and will make an example of thee”** — The physician speaks, who comes from heaven to heal the world and can cure all diseases. I will discover, that is, I will make you understand your errors, which before you thought were virtues; and to the nations which you sold in your fornication I will shew your nakedness, so that, seeing your foul body, by whose surface they were led before, they may cease to commit fornication with you; and to kingdoms, which are greater than nations, the shame you brought on yourself. And I will cast abominations upon thee, that is, I will show how abominable you ought to be to those who before were made one body with you; and I will make an example of thee, so that the likeness of the punishment may frighten men away from the likeness of the fault.
3.7:
**“And it shall come to pass that every one that shall see thee, shall flee from thee, and shall say: Ninive is laid waste: who shall bemoan thee?”** — Who will grieve over you?
**“whence shall I seek a comforter for thee?”**
• Whoever sees Ninive set as an example will be afraid and wonder.
• Whence could anyone be your comforter, when in your power you had mercy on no one, nor prepared anyone to share your mourning, you who would not have a partner in reigning?
**“And it shall come to pass”** — Mystically. He who is not ensnared by the false beauty of the world, and sees its foulness within, flees from it, and, judging all earthly goods worthy of lament, will say: Wretched is the world, which binds and holds so many men in vices. But who that understands this misery grieves with the world? As if to say: few there are who, even in their death, can be torn from the embraces of the beautiful harlot. Whence shall I seek a comforter? Who, discussing your unstable way of life, in which all things are wavering, can find anything in you from which he could bring you comfort?
3.8:
**“Art thou better than the populous Alexandria, that dwelleth among the rivers? waters are round about it”** — for it is girt on one side by the stream of the Nile, on another by the lake Mareotis, on the other side by the sea
**“the sea is its riches”** — is
**“the waters”** — are
**“Art thou better”**
• Art thou better than Alexandria, or more populous, or more powerful? She too will be taken by the king of Babylon, Nabuchodonosor, as you will. After this the site of Alexandria is described, which, set on the Nile and the sea, is surrounded on every side by waters.
• Allegorically. He rebukes the lover of the world. See how many peoples the Church contains, which dwells upon the rivers of the prophets, and has round about her teachers out of whose belly flow rivers; which are enriched by the spiritual sense of the law, which without faith in Christ is bitter; which has for walls the multitude of peoples, or of the Scriptures, which those once black and dark and dry make firm. But even she, if she does not attend to herself and keep her heart, will be led captive, and will lament her sons, who will be dashed in pieces before they come to the middle of the road; and the enemies, the devils, will hasten to divide among themselves by lot whatever is most splendid in her; and the great men, that is, those set over her, will be bound in the fetters of sins. How much more, then, will you unbelievers, who cling to the world, feel punishments and be despised? And you will seek help from the enemy, that the vices and demons may cease to pursue you; but all your strong holds, worldly sweetness, power, teachings, will be devoured by the devil, the eater, at the first shaking of the tree.
**“are its walls”** — The city which is now called Alexandria, after Alexander the Great, was before called No, the capital of Egypt; and this prophet called it by its old name, No, but the translator called it Alexandria, which was its name in his time.
3.9:
**“Ethiopia and Egypt were the strength thereof”** — that Ethiopia and Egypt and Africa are the defence of Alexandria the very position of the provinces and of the city shows; these peoples were allied
**“and there is no end”** — to her strength, or her wealth
**“Africa and the Libyans were thy helpers”** — O Alexandria
3.10:
**“Yet she also was removed and carried into captivity”** — The city I describe will be taken by the Babylonian king, and the same will lay waste both you and her.
**“young children”** — who could not walk
**“her”** — Alexandria's
**“were dashed in pieces”** — by the enemy
**“at the top”** — before their fathers' faces
**“of every street”** — at the crossroads
**“and they cast lots upon her nobles”** — the nobles will be divided by the victors' lot
**“and all her great men were bound in fetters”** — none of the princes will escape
3.11: **“Therefore thou also shalt be made drunk”** — Since Alexandria is to suffer these things, you too, O Ninive, once rich and beautiful, drinking of the same cup, will be made drunk, and, lying stupefied, will be despised by all; and, coming into such need, you will ask help from the Babylonians, or against the Babylonians from your enemies.
3.12: **“All thy strong holds”** — which you think impregnable, and your strong men, are compared to the first figs, which, moved by a light touch, fall without effort into the mouth of the eater, lest, if they fell on the ground, they should give labour to the one gathering them.
3.13:
**“Behold”** — O Ninive, no wonder if you are devoured so, since a people so unmanned cannot resist the enemy
**“thy people”** — as
**“are women”** — as weak as
**“in the midst of thee”** — therefore
**“the gates of thy land shall be set wide open to thy enemies”** — the city will be laid open to the enemy
**“the fire shall devour thy bars”** — with which the gates were shut
**“Behold thy people”**
• Morally. Ninive, which is called beautiful, signifies the soul, by nature fair, which, clinging to pleasures, is unmanned, and opens the gates of the senses to vices and demons. For if anyone is a lover of pleasures more than of God, he has opened the gates of his land to the enemy; and the bars of this Babylon will be consumed by fire, that is, the natural good of the soul, by which it could shut against the enemy the road of the bodily senses. To her it is said that she should draw to herself the water of the divine word as a wall, and hold fast the natural good of the soul as it were, so that the enemy may not break through to the inner parts. There follows: Go into the clay: that is, you who have entangled yourself in various evils, bear patiently the wrongs of temptation; otherwise you will perish and lose all your natural good. Against these things, multiply yourself in as great a number of virtues as is the number of the bruchus.
• Allegorically. O Ninive, your people, that is, all worldly men, are so enervated by vices that they have nothing manly. Hence the enemies, namely the demons, or the vices, have entered through the open bodily senses; and they also, like fire, devour the natural power of knowing God, which ought to have barred the gates of the senses. Against these evils draw water for yourself: sprinkle yourself with the word and with reason; exercise yourself in the knowledge of God through the virtues planted in you; and do penance for having fallen. This is what he says: Go into the clay: bear the wrong patiently, and the necessity of the body in which you are wrapped; and, working it, that is, bringing into servitude the brick, that is, the body, tread it and hold it, so that it does not rule over you; because, if you remain there, that is, in the body, the living flame either of the vices here, or of hell hereafter, will consume you; and you will perish by the sword, that is, by the violent assault of the devil. And, after the likeness of locusts, whatever seemed green in you, and the good of nature springing up of itself, is consumed by the bruchus eating it. But so that this may not happen, multiply yourself in virtues as innumerable as the bruchus. All these punishments you have suffered because you have multiplied your merchandises above the stars of heaven: because you gathered for yourself perishing riches by right and wrong; or you thought various teachings brighter than the stars; and, walking by the broad way, running to and fro in the softness of your opinion, you raised yourself to the heights; and your guards, that is, those set over you, were like locusts, raising themselves to the flight of heresy, but quickly falling down; and your little ones, that is, those born of the locusts, were like the attelebus, lifting themselves a little from the ground, so that at last they may grow into a locust. These, lacking the warmth of the true sun, sit on thorny seats, that is, the rough opinions of the philosophers. But when the sunrise comes, that is, the judgement of true knowledge, they leave their thorns and pass into pure and free flight.
3.14:
**“Draw thee water for the siege”** — so that those besieged may not lack drink
**“build up thy bulwarks”** — walls, towers
**“go into the clay, and tread, work it and make brick”** — make bricks, so that you may build up the breaches in the walls
3.15:
**“There shall the fire devour thee: thou shalt perish by the sword, it shall devour thee like the bruchus: assemble together like”** — as
**“the bruchus, make thyself many like the locust”** — and when you have done all these things, as the ground by the bruchus, so you will be devoured by the sword of a raging army
**“assemble together”** — And when you have been multiplied like the bruchus, and gathered into one like the locust, and have gathered riches like the stars of heaven: as the locust and the bruchus and the attelebus, which is the young of the locust, fly away when the sun grows warm and are not found, so you will be scattered and flee.
3.16:
**“Thou hast multiplied thy merchandises above the stars of heaven”**
• and
• as
**“the bruchus hath spread himself and flown away”** — its wings grown for flying
3.17:
**“Thy guards are like the locusts: and thy little ones like the locusts of locusts which swarm on the hedges in the day of cold: the sun arose, and they flew away, and their place was not known where they were”**
• because they cannot fly away
• but when
• warmed
• to other regions
• they do not remember the hedge on which they sat in the time of cold
• It is the nature of locusts to grow numb in the cold and to fly about in the heat.
• Further, the attelebus, with small wings, creeping rather than flying, consumes everything down to the dust wherever it springs up, because it cannot go away until its wings grow.
3.18:
**“have slumbered”**
• with the numbness of sloth
• Because your people are like women, and the gates are open to the enemy, and the whole multitude sitting on the wall is like locusts, which, as if at the dawning of the sun, at the coming of Nabuchodonosor, flee from the ramparts and do not return to their place; all of which God, angry, brought on you for laying waste his people; therefore your city is destroyed.
• Since up to here the ruin of the world has been spoken of, at the end the wound of the devil himself is spoken of, who was the prince of the world and boasted that he ruled in it; to whom this apostrophe is made: O Lucifer, you are crushed; destroyed is Ninive, your beautiful and powerful city, in which you set yourself even against the Son of God. The shepherds who fed the people, not for salvation but so that you might devour them, have failed. The crowd of the people that worshipped you, leaving you and your city, has fled to the hiding places of the mountains, that is, of the apostles, and there is none of your leaders to call back to himself the crowd that was once yours. Your wound has resounded through the whole world. All insult you who before were deceived by your tripping. For there is no one, or scarcely anyone, whom you have not at some time deceived. He in whom the malice of the devil does not stay, but passes, can insult him, and clap over him with good works as with outstretched hands.
**“Thy shepherds … O king of Assyria”** — the kings from other nations who served you
**“thy princes shall be buried: thy people are hid in the mountains, and there is none to gather them together”** — and, the princes who could have resisted being killed, the people was scattered in the wars, and none of the leaders could gather them and lead them back into battle.
3.19:
**“Thy destruction is not hidden, thy wound is grievous”** — because it cannot be cured by the physician's hand
**“all that have heard the fame of thee, have clapped their hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?”** — no one will give tears for your wound, because there is no one over whom your malice had not passed, which does not abide but passes.
**“all that have heard the fame”** — The nations oppressed by you, hearing of the death of the proud Assyrian and the destruction of the mighty city, will press their hands together in wonder at the unhoped-for news, or, insulting you for joy, will clap their hands.

1.1:
**“The burden”** — or: taking up
**“that … saw”** — understood
**“Habacuc”** — embrace, or embracing
**“The burden that … saw”** — Among the Hebrews “massa” is set down, that is, a heavy burden, because it presses on those against whom it is seen, and does not let them lift their necks.
1.2:
**“How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear?”** — crying out
**“shall I cry out”** — which is more
**“to thee”** — who are able to deliver
**“violence”** — of Nabuchodonosor and of the wicked
**“suffering”** — unjustly
**“and”** — yet
**“thou wilt not save?”** — though you are able
1.3:
**“Why”**
• therefore
• why do I live so long as to see countless evils?
**“hast thou shewn me iniquity”** — of the wicked
**“and grievance”** — of the good
**“to see rapine and injustice”** — of the wicked oppressing the good
**“before me?”** — who am innocent
**“and there is a judgment”**
• perverse
• Still the prophet speaks, or the people: that judgement is given against him not by truth but by power.
**“but opposition is more powerful”**
• than justice
• The common complaint of the saints to God: why do worldly judges, having taken gifts, condemn the innocent and free the guilty? And the princes of the Church too tear the law in pieces for gifts. But we ought not to be troubled at this, seeing that from the beginning of the world the just Abel was killed by the wicked Cain; Jacob was in exile while Esau reigned in his father's house. He too against whom this complaint is directed is crucified by the Jews, and Barabbas the robber is set free.
**“Jerome”** — Let no one wonder if what we have interpreted in the bad sense of the Chaldeans according to the letter seems, according to the tropological sense, to speak of clemency. History is strict and has no freedom to wander. Tropology is free, and bound only by these laws: that it follow piety, and the connection of the understanding and of the words; and that it not be violent in joining things that are much at odds with one another.
1.4:
**“Therefore the law is torn in pieces”** — gifts having been taken against the innocent, so that the sin of the rich man is defended rather than the truth of the poor
**“and judgment cometh not to the end”** — the end of judgement is to judge justly
**“because the wicked”** — Nabuchodonosor
**“prevaileth against the just”**
• Juda
• see the reason why he dares to say this
**“therefore”** — therefore I say, because
**“wrong judgment”** — It seems perverse that Josias, a just king, is slain by the king of Egypt; that Daniel and the three children serve while the Babylonian rules; and that Baltasar drinks among his concubines from the vessels of God.
1.5:
**“Behold ye”** — what is being done
**“among the nations, and see: wonder”** — those things before your own
**“and be astonished”** — at the greatness of the wonder
**“for a work is done”**
• so great as to silence your complaining
• it will be done in the crushing of other nations by the Chaldeans
**“in your days”** — so that you may see it
**“which no man”** — so great
**“will believe”** — to be going to happen
**“when it shall be told”**
• by anyone
• Allegorically. God threatens those who despise his providence, that he will raise up the worst angels, through whom he will bring torments either on sinful men or on the souls of the worst men. These are bitter and spare no one, and swift, quickly carrying out what is commanded; and they walk upon the breadth of the earth. The breadth of the earth is the carnal, because they go by the broad way to death. These the demons trample, so as to possess souls which by the merit of reason are God's, but by their fault become the devil's. He is terrible because of the many and various punishments he brings. But from himself, that is, from his own iniquity, he will be condemned. But if anyone, through penance, has turned from him to God, he will escape the burden, that is, the yoke of the devil; and, offering his back to God as rider, he will be swifter than wolves and leopards, that is, heretics and robbers; and the horsemen, that is, the demons themselves, whom he carried before, will be thrown off and dashed down. For these horsemen, that is, the devils, had come from afar, usurping a thing not their own; and when they have been thrown off, the horses, set free, not content with running, will take the flight of the eagle, so as to feed on the flesh of the word of God and make others one body with themselves; their face is like a burning wind, because no malice will be able to resist it. Then the divine word will gather into one faith all who were taken captive by the Chaldeans as the sand, and will triumph over the devil, or over wicked men cast down from his kingdom; and his princes will be a laughingstock: the power of the wicked, overcome, is turned to derision. He will laugh at every strong hold: whatever in the words or riches of the world is praised as high and strong, the word of God will destroy and mock, and will cast up a mount, by showing up its frailty. Then the spirit will be changed, so as not to punish as it had punished, but it will pass over sinners, praying for them and reconciling them to God. This is the strength of the divine word, or of Christ, which he has from his God for casting down all evils.
**“Behold ye among the nations”** — The voice of the Lord answering what was said before. As if to say: do not think this iniquity is brought by the Chaldeans on Israel alone, but also on all the nations round about; and see that the Chaldeans themselves will be so strong, and afterwards will fall, that if anyone foretold what is to come, it would seem incredible for the greatness of the thing.
1.6:
**“For behold, I”** — See the work he had said he would do.
**“will raise up the Chaldeans”**
• whose king is Nabuchodonosor
• evil angels, or men, who justly torment
**“a bitter … nation”** — cruel
**“and swift”** — to carry out the commands of God
**“marching”** — because, not content with its own borders
**“upon the breadth of the earth”**
• not only upon the Jews
• “Broad is the way that leadeth to destruction”; for the Chaldeans do not walk by the strait way “that leadeth to life”
**“the dwelling places”** — Its work is not to plough the land, but to live by plunder and possess cities not its own.
1.7:
**“They are dreadful, and terrible”**
• before it brings war, it carries terror in its face
• bringing dreadful punishments
**“from themselves”** — From its own nation, not from another, it will set up princes and powers, and its sword will have no attendants of other nations. Or: as it has done, so will it be done to it; as it laid waste, it will be laid waste.
1.8:
**“lighter”** — in pursuit
**“Their horses are … than leopards, and swifter than evening wolves”** — wolves are fiercer as night comes on, roused to madness by the day's hunger
**“and their horsemen shall be spread abroad: for their horsemen shall come from afar, they shall fly as an eagle”** — to which, as it flies, all things lie open below
**“that maketh haste to eat”** — not to fight, because no one will resist, but to range abroad
1.9:
**“They shall all come to the prey”** — not to battle
**“a burning wind”** — At whose breath all green things wither; so at the sight of the Chaldeans all things will be laid waste.
**“and they shall gather together captives as the sand”** — So great will be the number of the captives and of the spoil that it can, by hyperbole, be made equal to the sand
1.10:
**“And their prince shall triumph over kings, and princes shall be his laughingstock”** — because Nabuchodonosor will reign in the whole world, and will hold in derision the kings led before his chariot, and count them among his delights
**“and he shall laugh at every strong hold”** — cities fortified by the nature of the place and by the strength of men
**“he shall laugh at every”** — He will be of such pride that he will strive to overcome the nature of places and the strength of armies.
**“and”** — strong
**“shall cast up a mount”** — at Tyre, by casting a mound into the sea, he made an almost-island of an island
**“and shall take it”**
• the strong hold, or Tyre
• This is read more fully in Ezechiel.
1.11:
**“Then”** — when nothing has stood in his way
**“shall his spirit be changed”** — into pride, so that he believes himself to be God, making himself a golden statue
**“and”** — and after all this
**“he shall pass”** — into the figure of the beast
**“and fall”** — he will cease to be what he had been
**“this is his strength”** — Ironically. As if to say: this is his strength, which Bel his god gave him, to whose worship he forced everyone.
1.12:
**“Wast thou not from the beginning, O Lord my God”** — are you not then, O Lord my God, the author of these things?
**“my holy one”**
• who created us
• by whose clemency we subsist
**“and we shall not die?”**
• under so great an enemy
• with you protecting us
**“Lord, thou hast appointed him for judgment”** — to judge, so that he may be enemy and avenger, and through him you may correct whoever has sinned against you
**“and made him strong for correction”**
• as an executioner
• Nabuchodonosor, or the devil
• Lord, thou hast appointed him for judgment. Otherwise: a nation of demons is raised up against the unbelievers, bitter to punish; and it walks, present everywhere, wherever there is the breadth of the earth, to possess those in whom Christ ought to have dwelt. From itself shall its judgement and its burden proceed. But it is not broken until it has come to its fulfilment, weighed down by the greatness and weight of its iniquity. Its horses and horsemen, like leopards and wolves, thirst for blood and long for prey; and, while they are not expected, they come quickly from afar; they fly like the eagle that would set its nest among the stars, and hastens to its prey. For none of the demons spares; whatever they look on they want to burn; and the prince of the demons, like an eagle, will gather those deceived by his own, and will take them up from every side like sand; and many who seemed to exercise power mightily against him, by casting him out of possessed bodies, he will make subject to himself; and he will laugh; and whatever seems fortified and strong he will strive to overthrow. He will cast up a mount in earthly deeds and works; easily he will overthrow the strong hold. After this victory his spirit will be changed, and his mouth will pass even to heaven, because he will make himself God; and afterwards he will fall, and his ruin will show how strong his divinity was. The prophet, then, hearing that one so great is to be destroyed in this way, having complained that he, or those in whose person the prophet spoke, were just, now says coaxingly: Wast thou not from the beginning, O Lord? That we are not taken by so great an enemy is of your clemency. For you, O Lord, have appointed him as an executioner and made him strong, so that few or none can resist him.
• The prophet, understanding from the Lord's answer that Nabuchodonosor receives power against Juda, or the devil against believers, so that he may correct them, and that after the correction he himself too will be punished at the end, answers the Lord with the feeling of one coaxing and repenting: Lord, I did not know that Nabuchodonosor, or the devil, had received such power in the world, whose strength no one can resist; but yet your mercy lets us live among them.
• Allegorically. He returns to the general complaint, why, with God providing, the devil rules so much in the world; and it is joined to what goes before thus: I know, Lord, that with you protecting us we do not die, and that through the adversary, as through an executioner, you correct, you do not kill, and that nothing unjust pleases you; but yet I cannot find the cause why the unjust Cain killed the just Abel; why the whale devoured not only lesser fish but even the prophet Jonas. I do not say that anyone is just in your sight; but yet he who is afflicted is more just than he who afflicts; he ought therefore to have been subject to the more just. But since you are Lord of all, it must be that you do what cannot be done without you.
1.13:
**“Thy eyes are too pure”**
• whom nothing unclean pleases
• I know that you do not willingly look on evil, nor can anyone doubt your justice; but yet why do you suffer just Israel to be oppressed by the wicked Nabuchodonosor? Israel, even if not wholly just, is yet more just than its oppressor. As fish and the irrational animals, which have no ruler, lie under the strength of the stronger, so man, a rational being made in your image, cannot resist the bodily strength of the idolaters.
**“to behold evil, and thou canst not look on iniquity. Why lookest thou upon them that do unjust things, and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more just than himself?”** — The prophet knows that the angels of each one daily see the face of the Father, nor does he think anything ill of God; but he expresses human impatience in himself.
**“Why lookest thou upon the despisers”**
• you who alone look upon all things
• you do not avenge, who are just
**“and holdest thy peace”**
• nor do you even rebuke
• from rebuking
**“when … treadeth down”** — as if mud
**“the wicked”**
• Nabuchodonosor, or anyone
• as if to say: how ill this fits
**“the man that is more just than himself?”** — Juda, or anyone
1.14:
**“And thou wilt make men as the fishes of the sea, and as the creeping things”**
• you will leave them without care, without providence
• hence Boethius: “The acts of men alone thou spurnest”
**“that have no ruler”** — so the heretics lie
1.15:
**“all them”** — the human race, in Adam
**“He lifted up … with his hook”**
• Nabuchodonosor
• the devil
**“he drew them”** — from paradise
**“in his drag”** — by various and manifold deceit
**“and gathered them into his net: for this he will be glad and rejoice”**
• Nabuchodonosor, or the devil
• Allegorically. The devil, who lays waste all things, cast the hook to which Adam clung, and so drew him out of paradise with his net, and covered him with his drags, that is, with various deceits. So he will be glad that something other than the Lord's command prevailed; and he will sacrifice, not to the hook, which is understood as the perverse word, still set at the beginning, but to his net, because in it he has taken fat victims; for “by the disobedience of one man, many were made sinners,” and with Adam even the saints were cast out of paradise. Hence his food is choice; and because he deceived the first man, he does not cease to kill the whole human race.
• It can also be taken of the heretics, who with perverse and manifold teaching, as with hook and net and drags, catch many fish and take many creeping things. So they rejoice, and worship as God the word by which they were able to deceive and persuade; they cultivate it and polish it, knowing that by it they have killed so many victims and deceived so many of the powerful, whom he calls the fat portion and the choice food. So, like beasts that, having once tasted blood, always thirst for it, they spread the net, that is, all their effort, to kill more.
**“all them with his hook”** — Because he had named fish, he keeps the metaphor of fish: as the fisherman casts the hook, the net and the drag, so that the net may catch what the hook does not, and what escapes the net may be surrounded by the wider drag; so the Babylonians made the human race their prey.
1.16:
**“Therefore will he offer victims to his drag, and he will sacrifice to his net”** — to the idol he made in the plain of Dura, and to the image of Bel, to which, as to a great drag, he sacrificed fat victims, that is, forcing all the conquered nations to its worship
**“because through them”** — his idols
**“his portion is made fat, and his meat dainty”** — in his own opinion; for he will think he has riches when he subjugates princes and kings to his rule, whom he calls choice food
1.17:
**“For this cause therefore he spreadeth his net, and will not spare continually to slay the nations”**
• ceases
• Because he has once been glutted with a rich catch and has filled his drag, that is, his army, he does not cease to attack and slaughter the nations.

2.1:
To the first complaint the Lord had answered: Behold ye among the nations, and see: wonder, and be astonished. At these words the prophet, as if doing penance, tempered his question, saying: O Lord my God, my holy one, and we shall not die; but none the less, with veneration and praises of God, he went on asking: Thy eyes are too pure to behold evil, and thou canst not look on iniquity. Why lookest thou upon them that do unjust things? And what the devouring of the just man was, in what ways it was carried out, so that men became as the fishes of the sea, and the rest. Now, then, because he is a prophet, and says he doubts for this reason, that what is answered to him may be said to all, I will stand, he says, upon my watch, in the height of my prophecy, so that I may see what follows after the overthrow of the people and the temple.
**“I will stand upon my watch”** — I will keep my heart with all watchfulness
**“and fix my foot”** — the steadiness of the mind
**“upon the tower”** — Christ
**“and I will watch, to see what will be said to me, and what I may answer to him that reproveth me”** — the prophetic vision does not come to the prophets outwardly but in the inner man
**“and I will watch”** — And so I shall see what God answers me after my second question; and after he has answered me, and rebuked me for having complained wrongly, I shall see what I in turn ought to answer him.
**“to see”** — Human impatience, which we have in disputes, is elegantly described: before we know in what we are being refuted by the one answering, we are ready to answer, not as if from reason but from contentiousness. For if it were reason, the answer ought to have been awaited, and it seen whether one ought to answer or to agree with a reasonable saying.
2.2:
**“And the Lord answered me”** — While the prophet is still speaking, God is at hand, answering that the prophet should write plainly on tables, that is, on the broad hearts of the hearers.
**“Write”** — you who have spoken in the person of the doubting people
**“the vision”**
• the vision
• Write that vision: the vision, that is, the fulfilment of the vision.
**“and make it plain”** — make it clear
**“upon tables”** — in the breadth of hearts
**“that he that readeth it may run over it”**
• let it be darkened by no windings of riddles
• understanding without hindrance
• as if to say: because you are a prophet, I know that you are not ignorant, but I say it for others
• This is plainly a prophecy of the coming of Christ, and so the question set forth is answered: that until he comes iniquity will rule in the world and judgement will not come to the end. But the true Nabuchodonosor will take men like little fishes with net and drag, and the rational animal like a creeping thing that has no ruler.
• Hence: “In an accepted time have I heard thee.” And again: “When the fulness of the time was come, God sent his Son.”
2.3:
**“For as yet the vision”** — the vision
**“is far off”** — at the appointed time
**“and it shall appear at the end, and shall not lie”** — When the end of things has come, then he too will come, and the vision will be proved true by the plain showing of the thing
**“if it make any delay, wait for it: for it shall surely come”** — O reader, if, in your eagerness to see the vision, what is promised you seems slow to come, do not despair, but wait patiently for what I promise you; for it shall surely come, and so on.
**“and it shall not be slack”** — as far as it is itself concerned, though it may seem slow to you
2.4:
**“Behold, he that is unbelieving, his soul shall not be right in himself”**
• If anyone, because this promise is delayed, does not believe it will be fulfilled, he has not right faith in his heart
• on the contrary
• because he believes my promise
**“but the just shall live in”** — or: by
**“his faith”** — faith obtains this
**“shall live”**
• for ever
• this is the reward of faith
**“but the just … in his faith”** — The Apostle: “shall live by my faith.” But it should be noted that wherever a thing is written one way in the Hebrew and another in the Septuagint, the Apostle uses those testimonies which he had learnt from Gamaliel, the teacher of the law.
2.5:
**“And as wine deceiveth him that drinketh it”** — while it is being drunk it pleases and cheers, but afterwards that gladness is turned to ruin
**“so shall the proud man be”**
• Nabuchodonosor, believing himself great; or the devil, or Antichrist
• The coming of Christ and God's help having been promised to those who believe, Nabuchodonosor is shown to be deceived by his own pride.
**“the proud man”** — Allegorically. The proud devil, believing himself to be something, brings nothing to its end, because his attempts and labour will come to destruction; who, like hell and death, is not filled with the slain, and rejoices in deceiving all nations, and gathers to himself the peoples; and when they see him sent into Tartarus, seeing the parables of the prophets fulfilled in him, they will say with one voice of weeping: Woe to the devil, who multiplies what he did not bring forth.
**“and he shall not be honoured”** — he will not bring his will to its end
**“who hath enlarged his desire like hell”** — he is not filled with the slain
**“and is himself like death, and he is never satisfied”** — but, always greedy, he is in want
**“but will gather together”**
• so as to bring all down under his rule
• so as to confound all in one error
**“unto him all nations”** — nations, that is, the wicked
**“and heap together”** — as if they were lifeless things
**“unto him all people”**
• These things can also be understood of Antichrist, who, proud, sitting “in the temple of God, shewing himself as if he were God,” will kill many like hell, and will gather them to himself, leading them into his error. But afterwards, seeing him killed “with the spirit of” Christ's “mouth,” they will understand that what was said of him was true, and will say all that follows, with the same understanding that we have set out concerning the devil. All that shall be left of the people shall spoil thee: he calls those left the saints who did not serve Antichrist, by whom he will be spoiled for the iniquity which he practised over the whole earth, and for the laying waste of the city of the Church and the persecution of all who dwelt in it.
• By the name of the proud man the heretic too can be called, with a like explanation; heretics practise impiety in the Church. But the people that are left, that is, the men of the Church not deceived by their error, will suddenly rise up as if from a heavy sleep and bite them, and they will be a spoil to them.
2.6:
**“Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a dark speech concerning him?”** — By comparison with him who had laid waste the whole world, for whom the spoils of the whole world are not enough, they will deride the covetous
**“and it shall be said: Woe to him that heapeth together that which is not his own”** — what he did not bring forth
**“how long also doth he load himself”** — with the load of plunder; as if to say: weighing himself down with a heavy collar
**“with thick clay?”**
• elegantly, multiplied riches are compared to clay
• How long also doth he load, namely, until the day of judgement; and it is a rebuke, that through muddy works he loads on himself the weight of punishments. Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee? Either the angels, to whom the devil will be handed over for punishment, or those who, tempted by him, will do penance, converted to Christ; and they will be stirred up who tear you, those whom you had made drunk; they will lay waste your kingdom and divide the spoils of the beauty of the house; because you stripped the Jewish people of the garments I had given them, therefore the peoples left, who were not subject to your kingdom, will spoil you, because you shed the blood of many nations; and it will return on your head, and the impiety of the land of the Jews, and of the city of Jerusalem and its inhabitants, who said: “Crucify him, crucify him.”
2.7:
**“Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee: and they be stirred up that shall tear thee”** — those lying in wait for you will awake
**“Shall they not rise up”** — The Medes and Persians, destroying the Babylonian empire, will first bite and afterwards tear; Nabuchodonosor will be a spoil to them, and the waster of the world will be spoiled by the peoples who were able to escape his hand; and this will be done to him because of the blood of Juda and the iniquity of the land of Israel and of Jerusalem and of the whole people of the Jews.
2.8:
**“Because thou hast spoiled many nations, … shall spoil thee”** — they will pay like for like
**“all that shall be left of the people … because of men's blood”** — of Juda
**“and for the iniquity of the land”** — of promise
**“of the city”** — Jerusalem
2.9:
**“Woe to him that”** — who greedily aims to possess kingdoms or riches
**“gathereth together … covetousness”** — which is the cause of ruin
**“an evil … to his house, that his nest may be on high”** — where he may sleep safely
**“and thinketh he may be delivered”** — through avarice and pride
**“out of the hand of evil”**
• from the power of the enemy
• Woe to him that gathereth together. Allegorically. When the word is directed to the devil, or to Antichrist, or to the heretic. There is a good covetousness of the Church's teacher, who by studious labour always longs to make more disciples for himself. But woe to him who greedily gathers perverse conventicles to his house, and promises his followers that they will possess the kingdom of heaven with him and not feel the fires of hell. For their counsel will be the confusion and disgrace of their house, when the end of things shows that the promise was false. This perverse teacher, the more he has in his company, the more he sins against his own soul. Finally, the stones of his church, that is, those deceived by him, will show the covetousness of the proud man, that he has deceived all nations by his persuasion. And the wood of the Lord's cross, at which the two walls are joined, will speak of their teaching. For they cannot persuade otherwise unless they put forward the glory of the cross before their perversity.
**“Woe to him that gathereth together”** — Still the word is to him who does not understand that gathered riches are the cause of the ruin of his house; and it accuses him too of pride, that like a bird he sets his nest on high and does not think he will come into the hands of his enemies.
2.10:
**“Thou hast devised confusion”**
• not salvation
• but proud and arrogant thinking has disgrace for its end
**“to thy house, thou hast cut off many people, and thy soul hath sinned”** — and you raged with the desire of killing others, and ran riot with such cruelty that, if it may be said, the stones of the city and the timbers of the overthrown walls cry out your fierceness
2.11: **“For the stone shall cry out of the wall: and the timber that is between the joints of the building, shall answer”** — which is set in the middle of the structure to hold the walls together
2.12:
**“Woe to him that buildeth a town”** — Babylon
**“Woe to him that buildeth”**
• Still he speaks against Nabuchodonosor, who builds the walls of Babylon with the ruins and deaths of many peoples. Hence follows the vengeance sent by God.
• Allegorically. The devil and Antichrist and the heretic build their church by the destruction of those deceived, and prepare a city of iniquities, that is, by setting their mouth against heaven. But is such a building from the Lord? No; for, though countless nations are led into their error, yet they will fail so that they cannot be compared with the multitude of the Church. But either they will fail and be punished with the fire of their prince, or surely they will be set on fire with the fire which Christ came to cast on the earth; and so the earth will be filled with the glory of God by those who repent, when “their sound hath gone forth into all the earth”: as waters covering the sea, so that the waters of God may cover all the bitterness which the earth had drunk when the devil rained it, so that it can no longer appear.
2.13:
**“Are not these things from the Lord of hosts?”** — Truly from the Lord are these things that follow: namely, that the peoples will labour in vain when Babylon is set on fire, and the peoples of the Chaldean nation will fail.
**“for the people shall labour in a great fire: and the nations in vain, and they shall faint”** — and for these evils, such vengeance
2.14:
**“For the earth shall be filled, that men may know the glory of the Lord”** — When Babylon has been burnt and overthrown, the might of God's power will be made plain to all
**“as waters covering the sea”** — as the waters cover the bed and floor of the sea, so the glory of the Lord will fill all things
2.15:
**“Woe to him that giveth drink to his friend, and presenteth his gall, and maketh him drunk, that he may behold his nakedness”**
• the metaphor of a drunk man disgraced by his nakedness
• Sedecias, as the Hebrew says, blinded by Nabuchodonosor in Reblatha, that is, Antioch, and led to Babylon, one day at a crowded feast was given a drink to loosen his bowels, and, brought in before the faces of the feasters, was suddenly loosed in a flux of the bowels. Hence God threatens Nabuchodonosor himself that he will drink such a drink, and suffer all that Sedecias suffered.
**“Woe to him that giveth drink”**
• Still he inveighs against Nabuchodonosor, because, forgetting that he was a man, he gave gall and bitterness to drink to another man.
• It should be known that this passage, Woe to him that giveth drink to his friend, and those in which it is said, Woe to him that heapeth together that which is not his own, and Woe to him that gathereth together an evil covetousness, and so on, and Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and so on, can equally be taken, both according to the history and according to the anagogy, against Nabuchodonosor, or the devil, or Antichrist, or the heretic.
• Allegorically. Woe to you, devil, or Antichrist, or heretic, who with muddy teaching make drunk those you deceive, so that you may see them naked of faith and good works, and filled with the disgrace of errors and evil works, who before were glorious in the image of God. But, O devil or heretic, who think you have a golden cup, drink you too of the cup that is in the hand of God, full of new wine, and fall fast asleep: that is, cease from your former opinion, and do not think firm the things in which you stood before; because the cup of the right hand of the Lord will compass you, the vengeance sent by God, and shameful vomiting on your glory: the glory which you had unjustly swallowed you will vomit up with disgrace. And this you will suffer because the iniquity of Libanus will cover you. Libanus is called incense, by which you understand the worship of God: because you do not worship God rightly, you will be confounded. Hence: “and may his prayer be turned to sin.” And the ravaging of beasts will terrify you: when you see those whom you laid waste and dragged into error suffer torments, then you will be terrified because of the blood of men and the iniquity of the land. Because I named Libanus and beasts, lest you think I am speaking of brute creatures, I tell you plainly: you will suffer punishments because of the blood of the men whom you made to perish to God; and you practised impiety in the land of the living and the meek, and in the city of the Church of God, and you made many dwelling in it sharers in your impiety.
**“Woe to him that giveth drink to his friend”** — Here the friend is understood either as Sedecias, or as any man made drunk by the evils of Nabuchodonosor, so that Nabuchodonosor might see the nakedness of Sedecias and of all the captives, that is, all of them stripped and captive, and once glorious, brought down to the disgrace of slavery.
2.16:
**“Thou art filled with shame instead of glory”** — Whoever drinks your cup, O Nabuchodonosor.
**“drink”** — the cup of God.
**“thou also”** — you who have made others drunk
**“and fall fast asleep: the cup of the right hand of the Lord shall compass thee”** — the vengeance of God's power
**“and shameful vomiting shall be on thy glory”**
• you will vomit up what you had swallowed
• from the height of glory you will be brought to the last evils
2.17:
**“For the iniquity of Libanus shall cover thee”** — Your pride, and the overthrow of the temple, and the plundering of the sanctuary, will lay you waste; and all this you will suffer because you laid waste Juda, overthrew the land of promise and the city of Jerusalem and all its inhabitants.
**“For the iniquity of Libanus”** — Because he had once named Libanus, under its figure he compares to animals or beasts the victims and sacrifices, or the multitude of the peoples that was killed in Jerusalem, saying: And the ravaging of beasts shall crush thee.
**“and the ravaging of beasts”** — when you see them in punishment
**“shall terrify them”** — elsewhere: thee
**“because of”** — for
**“the blood of men”** — of Juda
**“and the iniquity of the land, and of the city”** — of the Church, or of Jerusalem
2.18:
**“What doth the graven thing avail”** — graven in stones, molten in metals.
**“What doth … avail”**
• He speaks against all idolaters, and especially against Nabuchodonosor, wondering at the folly of the king who ordered a golden statue to be set up in the plain of Dura; and the maker trusts in the image he has made.
• What does it avail to adore a graven thing? This I say because its maker has graven it with art. And what does it avail to adore a molten thing and a false image? And this I say because its maker has trusted in a thing of his own forging, to make dumb idols.
**“because the maker thereof hath graven it, a molten, and a false image? because the forger thereof hath trusted in a thing of his own forging, to make dumb idols”** — Allegorically. Perverse teachings, which are adored by their makers, are compared to the graven and the molten thing. The carving made in stone is understood in those teachings which show their folly at first sight; the casting made in metals, in those where there seems to be some reason of worldly wisdom; for, as with gold, so with the learning of the philosophers and the splendour of eloquence, the idol is cast. So the forged thing will not profit its maker, because the dumb and deaf image does not hear its worshipper.
2.19:
**“Woe to him that saith to wood: Awake: to the dumb stone: Arise: can it”** — the stone
**“teach? Behold, it”** — stone
**“is laid over”**
• elsewhere: covered
• it has been made
**“with gold, and silver, and … spirit”**
• holy and good; when “spirit” is put without anything added, it is understood of the Holy Spirit
• no spiritual grace, no power is in them
**“there is no … in the bowels thereof”**
• an unclean spirit can attend on images, but it cannot be within
