• Allegorically. In all the idols of the heretics and the inventions of the devil there is no grace of the Holy Spirit; but, though they seem to show forth the image of divinity and the beauty of teachings, there is nothing in them breathing and alive.
• Or spirit, that is, wind; for “ruah” among the Hebrews means both, both soul and wind, and both are denied to the idols.
**“Woe to him that saith to wood”** — Human error is described, which, for the brightness of the material, thinks gods the gold, silver, gems and silk with which the idols are smeared or covered; to which the craftsman can give form but cannot give life. But on the contrary, the Lord is in his holy temple, that is, in the Son, or in heaven, or in the soul of the just, or in the creation of the whole world.
2.20:
**“But the Lord is in his holy temple: let … keep silence”**
• or: let it keep silence
• or: let it leap

3.1:
**“A PRAYER OF HABACUC”** — The Septuagint: A prayer with a canticle; for he prays for the coming, and so rejoices and praises God, both the Father who sends and the Son who is sent.
**“A PRAYER OF HABACUC THE PROPHET FOR IGNORANCES”** — A prayer of Habacuc for ignorances, because, erring about the judgements of God, he had rashly said: How long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear? and: Why lookest thou upon them that do unjust things, and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more just than himself? Now, understanding from God's answer that Nabuchodonosor, or the devil, or Antichrist, has been set up to correct the nations, he does penance and asks pardon for what he did in ignorance; or he prays that through the coming of Christ the error of men, which comes from ignorance, may be taken away, and, the shadow removed, the truth be given. Nor is it a prayer as if about uncertain things, but a sure prophetic declaration. Others have: for things done willingly, because the prophet sinned under no necessity but willingly, thinking ill of God's judgement; or he prophesies that the nations will believe willingly in him whom he promises is to come.
**“A PRAYER OF HABACUC … FOR IGNORANCES”** — Habacuc means “embrace,” because he loved the Lord and joined himself to him; or “wrestling.” This is Jerome's translation from the Hebrew, which is expounded here. The Septuagint differs greatly here from all the others, both in words and in sense; little will be set down here according to it.
3.2:
**“O Lord, I have heard thy hearing”** — that God is man
**“and was afraid”**
• because it is wonderful
• but
• O Lord, I have heard. Historically: I have heard the punishments you have prepared for the devil and for Nabuchodonosor; and as I was terrified that the devil will be so pierced through, so I pray: fulfil what you have promised, and when the time is complete give the Christ you have promised; let it not die void, but bring it to life, that is, fulfil it. This can also be taken of the resurrection: that he who died for us may be brought to life.
• According to the Septuagint: O Lord, I have heard your word in the Scriptures with the inner ear, and have considered your works, so that from the creatures I might understand the creator, and through them I was astonished; losing the sense of man, I was turned to a holy madness; or, troubled with wonder, I broke out into your praise, saying: In the midst of two living creatures thou shalt be known: that is, through the Son and the Holy Spirit the Father is understood; or the two cherubim, who look toward each other and have the oracle between them; or the two seraphim, of whom one cries to the other the mystery of the Trinity, one of whom, sent, cleanses the lips of the prophet, and says: “I am come to cast fire on the earth; and what will I, but that it be kindled?” But simply: Christ was recognised between two thieves; or by the Jews and the Gentiles, surrounding him on either side; or between the two Testaments, which breathe life.
**“O Lord, I have heard”** — The Septuagint: O Lord, I have heard thy hearing, and was afraid; O Lord, I have considered thy works, and was astonished; in the midst of two living creatures thou shalt be known.
**“O Lord, thy work”** — is
**“in the midst of the years bring it to life”**
• in the fulness of time
• when the time of fulfilment has come, you will show to be true what you promised
**“In the midst of the years thou shalt make it known”**
• your work
• and
**“when thou art angry”** — he does not say “when you have inflicted punishment”; one who is angry sometimes does not strike
**“thou wilt remember mercy”**
• you threatened so as to frighten
• as if forgetting, while he put it off
3.3:
**“God will come from the south”**
• “Out of Egypt have I called my son.”
• from Theman, which means “from the south”; so he will come from the noonday, from the children of clear light
• The knowledge of God the Father comes to those who are worthy, in full light; and the knowledge of the holy one, that is, of the Son of God, will come from the mount, and so on: that is, from the Father, who is full of powers and protects and cherishes all things; or from the height of a shady and dense utterance, woven together from many testimonies. Or: Pharan means “the mouth of one seeing,” and the knowledge of the Son comes from the word of a learned man. Or: he will come, that is, he will be born in Bethlehem, which lies to the south; and because he it is who gave the law on Sinai, he will come from Pharan, which is a place near mount Sinai.
**“and the holy one from mount Pharan”**
• shady and dense
• always, or: diapsalma
• Sela in Hebrew; Jerome: always; the Septuagint: diapsalma. Always: that is, he who was born in Bethlehem, who gave the law on Sinai, is the author for all things past, present and to come.
**“His glory covered the heavens”** — he sat at the right hand of the power of God
**“and the earth is full of his praise”**
• “His word runneth swiftly”
• because “how admirable is thy name in the whole earth”
• His glory covered. At the coming of Christ all things were filled with glory. Hence: “Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will”; and: making peace both as to the things that are in heaven, and the things on earth.
3.4:
**“His brightness shall be as”** — as
**“the light”** — because his brightness too shone like the Sun of justice
**“horns are in his hands”**
• the trophies of the cross
• Horns are often put for kingdoms; or: after his miracles had grown or shone out, his hands will be fixed on the horns of the cross.
**“There”** — in the horns themselves
**“is his strength hid”** — He “humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death.”
3.5:
**“Death shall go before his face”**
• he will destroy death
• Death shall go: that is, the devil will meet him as he comes out of baptism, and will stand before his feet, to tempt him for forty days.
**“And the devil shall go forth before his feet”** — when he enters, the devil flees
3.6:
**“He stood and measured the earth”**
• he will stand and measure; he will divide from these those whom he will take up
• The Saviour, standing and measuring all things with his eye, scatters the nations and crushes the mountains and hills of the world. Or: the mountains are the demons.
**“He beheld, and melted”** — from ice
**“the nations: and the ancient mountains were crushed to pieces”** — not of God
**“The hills of the world were bowed down”** — which before his coming were upright, whose pride no one could humble
**“by the journeys of his eternity”**
• through the preachers
• of God; because eternity came to us through the flesh; or it always came, from the beginning of the world, to the saints, through whom it bowed down the way of the proud
3.7:
**“I saw … for their iniquity”** — or: he saw
**“the tents of Ethiopia”** — the same as the tabernacles of the Ethiopians, that is, of the demons
**“the curtains of the land of Madian shall be troubled”**
• For iniquity, or for labours: because those who labour for riches or honours become a lodging for demons, who ought to have been a temple of God; so they are troubled, because, made high, they always fear death and judgement. Madian means “hearing,” because they are already tormented with fear of the judgement.
• And I saw long before that the tents of Ethiopia will be troubled, and this for iniquity; and the curtains, that is, the tents, of the land of Madian will be troubled; and this will happen when the rivers have been changed. The Old Testament passes into the New; with its hearers washed in the Red Sea, you are no longer angry; or: in the sea, that is, the world, you, I say, who ride.
• The black Ethiopians, who feed on the flesh of the dragon, are the demons; whoever in this world labours for honours and riches becomes their tabernacle; and when he has gained them, he gives himself to luxury and pleasures, so that luxury consumes what avarice gathered. Such a man, for his labours, becomes a lodging of demons. But after he has been enriched and exalted, then, from the consciousness of his sins, he will always dread death and judgement, and will bear with daily fear the torments he knows he has deserved.
3.8:
**“Wast thou angry … with the rivers?”**
• the prophet asks
• This is to say briefly, according to the letter: as you dried up the Jordan and the Red Sea, fighting for us (for you are not angry with things without sense), so now, mounting your chariots and taking up your bow, you will give salvation to the people, and what you swore to the fathers and the tribes of the people for ever.
• It is said ambiguously. If the rivers and the sea are bad, God is angry and strikes them: the eloquence of the heretics is a river, they who are carried about with every wind of doctrine and always toss with malice; they are the sea, against which the onset of the Lord is made, so that they may feel his coming and know within what bounds they are shut in. If they are good, Jesus is praised, or lifted up, in them, and he sets his Church upon such a sea.
**“Wast thou angry, O Lord, with the rivers? or was thy wrath upon the rivers? or … in the sea?”** — The words of God that are plainer and give drink are called rivers; the sacraments, the deep sea.
**“thy indignation”** — or: onset
**“Who”**
• or: for
• or: who
**“will ride”** — or: will ride
**“upon … horses”** — the apostles
**“thy horses: and thy chariots”** — the four evangelists
**“upon thy horses”** — The souls of the saints. Riding in these chariots, he goes through the whole world, and bends his bow and does not at once let fly, so that he who has just been terrified may not feel the shot; and this he does always. For always he sits armed in the saints and runs about for the salvation of the world; and through this you will divide and scatter the rivers of the earth that fight against your people. Or: the earth will be split by rivers, as in an earthquake new springs flow out and others are stopped up; so, the world being shaken by the coming of Christ, the springs of Israel were stopped up and the apostles flowed out. As the veins of the body hold blood, so the veins of the lands hold hidden waters, which break out when they are shaken; so too the soul has waters by nature, but hidden through sloth; shaken by the word of God, they break out. These are the wells of Abraham, which the Philistines stop up.
3.9:
**“surely”** — or: bending
**“Thou wilt … take up thy bow”** — the Scriptures are revealed
**“according to the oaths which thou hast spoken to the tribes”** — and so you will fulfil the oaths promised to the tribes and the fathers
**“Thou wilt divide the rivers of the earth”**
• Always, or: diapsalma
• You will scatter the wisdom of the world; and the proud peoples will see this and grieve; but yet the apostolic teaching has passed into all the earth; the wicked indeed rise up against it
• Thou wilt divide the rivers of the earth: because the Lord took up his bow to fulfil the oaths he spoke to the tribes, it is fittingly said: you will divide the rivers of the earth, you will part and scatter those fighting against your people.
3.10:
**“saw”** — as the rivers flowed
**“thee”** — O God
**“and were grieved”** — to penance
**“The mountains”**
• the powerful of the world
• and then
**“the great body”** — the onset and persecution.
**“the great body of waters passed away”** — There are everlasting waters, which flow from the springs of Israel; there are short-lived ones, which flow into the sea, whose end is destruction: these are the heresies, which flourish for a time.
**“the great body of waters”** — Their onset and persecution ceased; and then the deep, that is, the dead, praised you; then too the high ones, that is, the angels, showed forth the victor as with the applause of lifted hands.
**“The deep put forth its voice”** — or: the wise are the deep
3.11:
**“The sun and the moon”**
• those through whom he gave light to the people
• the sun and the moon: Christ and the Church
• The sun and the moon: your sun and moon, which were covered by the weight of evils and the error of darkness, received back their first light.
**“stood still in their habitation, in the light of thy arrows”** — of the preachers
**“they shall go”**
• the peoples
• the apostles
**“in the brightness of thy glittering spear”**
• of Christ, who is called “a chosen arrow”
• In the light of thy arrows. The arrows are lighter, the spear greater.
• The arrows are the strokes of God, the spear his teaching.
3.12:
**“In thy anger”** — In the preaching of the apostles, who were even thought to be mad
**“In thy anger thou wilt tread … under foot”** — When you avenge the wrong done to your people, you will trample the earthly kingdoms and make all the nations wonder, because you went forth for the salvation of your people, and came to them with your Christ; at whose coming you struck Antichrist in this world, which “is seated in wickedness,” or the devil himself, who is the head of impiety, whom he cast out of his lodging so that justice might dwell there.
3.13:
**“Thou wentest forth”** — Thou wentest forth, because they could not come in to you.
**“for the salvation of thy people”** — from the majesty, or the ceremonies, of the Jews, and from the temple; hence: “your house shall be left to you, desolate.”
**“for salvation with thy Christ”** — so that they may offer their necks to Christ the rider
**“Thou struckest the head of the house of the wicked”** — from the world
**“Thou struckest the head”** — As Christ is the head of the Church and of every man, so of all the demons who fight in this world the head is Beelzebub, the prince of the devils; and each of their troops has its heads and princes. For example, the spirits of fornication have their own chief; the spirits of vainglory, the spirits of lying, the spirits of unbelief have commanders of their army. But God, most merciful, where there had been the worst head, often cuts it off and puts in its place the best head. The Hebrews hand down that Reseph is the name of a demon who holds the chief place among the others, and who, for his great swiftness and his running in every direction, is called a bird and a flying thing; and that he it was who spoke to the woman in paradise under the figure of the serpent, and from the curse by which he was condemned by God received the name Reseph, which means “creeping on the belly.”
**“thou hast laid bare his foundation”**
• Thou hast laid bare. The Septuagint: Thou hast raised up bonds even to the neck, to the end; so that, the former yoke laid down, we may take on the bonds of charity, the light yoke, in the chariot of Christ. Here, for sela, they were forced to put “to the end.”
• Thou hast laid bare his foundation: that is, you have made his hidden things open, not for a short time but for ever.
• The foreigners had covered over with earth the foundation of Christ, which is in the soul; but, the earth thrown out, the best foundation is laid bare, or adorned, as others put it, so that it may appear and receive back its brightness; and this for ever.
**“of the wicked”** — The wicked man is either Nabuchodonosor or every adversary of the people of God; and you cursed not only the sceptres but also the head, which you had struck, of the warriors who came like a whirlwind to scatter, that is, to overthrow Israel and take it captive; and they exult, devouring poor Israel subject to them, as if they did it in secret, that is, without your knowing. So you came to battle for your people, and, sending your chariots into the waters, that is, into many nations, you made them a way in the mud, that is, so that you may trample them and crush them like mud.
**“even to the neck”**
• so that they may offer their necks to Christ the rider
• always
3.14:
**“Thou hast cursed”** — by diminishing
**“his sceptres”** — the kingdoms
**“like that of him that devoureth the poor man”** — But as vainly as one who kills a poor man whom he thinks rich.
**“the head of his warriors, them that came out as a whirlwind to scatter me. Their joy was like that of him that devoureth the poor man in secret”** — “He sitteth in ambush with the rich in private places.”
3.15:
**“a way”** — these having been destroyed
**“Thou madest … in the sea”** — of this world, where the mud of cares is
**“for thy horses, in the mud of many waters”** — I have heard: in his own person, of the whole people.
3.16:
**“I have heard”** — what was foretold
**“and my bowels were troubled”** — lest I should endure the like
**“at the voice”** — namely, yours
**“my lips trembled”**
• the fear of the mind is shown in the mouth.
• I have heard and … were troubled. I too heard through the Spirit what the horses will suffer, and my flesh trembled, and at this voice my lips trembled.
**“Let rottenness enter into my bones”**
• but
• Let … enter. Now we gladly suffer all distresses, and tremble with our whole being at your threat; and not only this, but I seek it of my own accord: Let it enter.
• Into my bones. Not only into the flesh but even into the marrow of the bones; and, laid low by the rottenness of the body, let it swarm with worms, so that, when I have borne all the distresses of the captivity for my sins, I may rest with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and the others who are the people that are girded. This is allegory, so that the allegory is mixed with history; for sometimes the history itself is woven metaphorically, and its metaphor does not always speak an allegory. According to the history, he says in the person of the people that he gladly suffers anything in the captivity, so that he may rest at the time when he curses the sceptres of the wicked and the horses tread the mud, so that afterwards he may return with the saints Zorobabel and Jesus to the land of promise; but the letter of the book does not mean this.
**“and swarm under me”** — that is, I will gladly suffer what Job suffered
**“That I may rest”** — at the end of the world
**“in the day of tribulation”**
• of evils
• “That day is a day of wrath, … a day of calamity and misery”
• Of tribulation, because then all things will be taken from man, according to the saying: “when he shall die he shall take nothing away; nor shall his glory descend with him.”
**“that”** — or: and
**“I may go up”** — for the just man always goes up
**“to our people that are girded”**
• the strong warrior
• this he dares to say when in tribulation
• The prophet, seeing here the destruction of the enemies by God's victory, turns back to himself, saying that he would rather be afflicted with the just than be tormented for ever with the wicked.
3.17:
**“For the fig tree shall not blossom: and there shall be no spring in the vines”** — The fig tree. So I want to suffer here, and afterwards go up to the people that are girded, because the day of tribulation will come, and, while the rest are set in distress, I shall rejoice in your majesty. Or: when the day of the Jews' overthrow comes, I, while the people perishes, am chosen, and shall join myself to the disciples of Christ, going up into the mountains, because he teaches them on a mountain, the crowds left below. For the fig tree to which he came hungry, that is, the people of the Jews, gives no fruit, and so it is cursed; and it bears no fruit, not for ever and ever, but until the age, that is, until the Gentiles have come in. This is the fig tree for which the husbandman pleads, that is, Gabriel or Michael, to whom the people of the Jews has been entrusted, who prays at the Passion: give them time for penance, and do not cut it down; and if it bear fruit (the fig tree is to be understood as left in suspense)… you will move it to another vineyard, that is, the Church. He came three times: through the law, through the prophets, through himself. After the Passion, penance having been granted for forty-two years, because it bore no fruit, it was overthrown. Those who were converted were moved over to the people of the Gentiles, to which the prophet goes up. The vine, that is, the people, which bore no fruit but thorns; not judgement but a cry, saying: “Crucify him, crucify him,” and “We have no king but Caesar”; which after the servants killed the son; and so “the boar out of the wood hath laid it waste.” The olive, that is, the people, whose branches were broken and the wild olive grafted in. Or: the fig tree is the Holy Spirit, for the sweetness of its fruit; the vine Christ, who says: “I am the true vine”; the olive the Father, from whom is all light. In the book of Judges the trees of the forests are said to have come to these trees, that they might reign over them, which never happens; but the bramble rules them, which has thorns and fire, to wound and burn up the fields. Jerusalem, once on the holy mountains, is now called a plain, which feeds not only no rational beings, but not even the cattle and oxen that would carry the yoke of God. All these things will be taken away from the people, because it acted wickedly against God. But if you take the day of tribulation of the end, you will refer it all to those who say they are of the Church but have no works; and the fig tree, the vine, the olive, that is, the Trinity, will not give them its fruit; and not only have they no grain for men, but not even food for cattle and beasts; and instead of the mountains they dwell in the low place.
**“The labour of the olive tree shall fail: and the fields shall yield no food: the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls”** — It promises one thing, “All that the Lord hath spoken we will do,” and does another
3.18: **“But I will rejoice in”** — The prophet says this, the Jews being scattered over the world, in the person of the believers. But if you take it of the end, it will be said thus: as, when Egypt was struck, the fig tree, the vine, the olive and the fields gave no fruit, and the cattle failed because they had no food, and Israel exulted; so at the end of the world, when charity grows cold and does not give the fruits of works, then the just man, glad, will say: But I will rejoice in the Lord; and, brought out to the summit, I will sing the triumph; I who at the beginning said, I shall cry, and thou wilt not hear; who complained of his justice and judgement, will praise his equity.
3.19:
**“The Lord God is my strength”**
• not the justice of the law
• nothing else
**“and he will make my feet”** — so that I may tread upon the asp and the basilisk
**“like the feet of harts”** — he will set me among the others who have the virtue of the hart
**“and he the conqueror will lead me upon my high places”** — who first conquered in the contest
**“singing psalms”** — among the angels I will sing his triumph, and on earth peace to men.

1.1:
**“The word of the Lord”** — that is
**“that came to Sophonias the son of Chusi”** — my Ethiopian, or: lowliness
**“the son of Godolias”** — the greatness of God
**“the son of Amarias”** — the word of the Lord
**“the son of Ezechias”** — the strength of the Lord
**“in the days of Josias”** — the lifting up of the Lord
**“the son of Amon king of Juda”**
• the faith of the king
• He prophesies the overthrow of Jerusalem and the captivity of Juda and Benjamin by Nabuchodonosor; a captivity seen to begin once Josias was slain, for his sons and grandsons are not to be thought to have reigned so much as to have been made a mockery by the Egyptian king and the Chaldeans, and tormented by various misfortunes. And since this captivity hung over the people for their crimes, lest the people say they were driven to idolatry by wicked kings, a just king was given them; and because the people persevered in the worship of idols while he was zealous with the zeal of the Lord, the Lord sets forth the just cause of his anger.
• Sophonias: a watchtower, or a secret. For he was set in a watchtower and on high, according to that: “Son of man, I have made thee a watchman to the house of Israel.” And he knew the mysteries of God. Whence: the Lord will not do anything unless he reveal it to his prophets.
• Amon, that is, faith. Manasses, after many crimes, and after the captivity, did penance in Babylon, whereby he obtained God’s mercy; and so, as a token of the faith with which he had believed God, he called his son Amon.
**“The word of the Lord that”** — In the title the prophet’s lineage and time are noted. Among the names of his fathers is set Chusi, which is interpreted “my Ethiopian”; in which it is noted that he who was once an Ethiopian has turned to penance. As it is said: “Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands to God.” And rightly Sophonias, as the son of an Ethiopian, writes in what follows of the Ethiopians’ penance, saying: “From beyond the rivers of Ethiopia” they shall bring me offerings. In the days of Josias: just as those whom Elias enlightened are called the days of Elias, so those who lifted themselves up to God are the days of Josias, for Josias means “the lifting up of the Lord”, and he was a just man. And note at the same time that here no kings of Israel are set down, but only the kings of Juda, because the ten tribes had already been taken captive by the Assyrians under Ezechias.
1.2: **“Gathering, I will gather together all things from off the face of the land, saith the Lord”** — I will no longer grant a place for penance, but I will consume all things from the face of the land
1.3:
**“I will gather man, and beast, I will gather the birds of the air, and the fishes of the sea”** — gathering man and beast
**“I will gather man, and beast”** — Even the brute animals will feel God’s anger: when the cities are overthrown and the men slain there will be a wilderness and a scarcity of beasts and birds; and this is because the multitude of the ungodly was too great, and so they will be laid waste. It can also be taken of the consummation of the world, when men and beasts and all things will fail, and iniquity will be taken away from the face of the land.
1.4:
**“And I will stretch out my hand”** — the stretching out of the hand shows the gesture of one who strikes
**“upon Juda, and upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem: and I will destroy”** — I will take away
**“out of this place the remnant”** — the keepers of Baal, the few who were left from the slaughter by the enemy
**“of Baal”** — the idol of the Sidonians
**“and the names of the wardens of the temples”**
• who were the authors of idolatry
• He calls the priests of idols wardens of the temples: those who in God’s temple worshipped idols and God alike.
**“And I will stretch out”** — After the ruin of the ungodly and the taking away of the wicked, the Lord speaks against Juda and Jerusalem. For Juda and Benjamin set up a statue of Baal in the Lord’s temple, and in the same sanctuary worshipped idols and God together. And so he calls the priests of idols not priests but temple-wardens and fanatics.
**“with the priests”**
• that is, I will destroy those who were once priests of the Lord, and now worship God and idols together
• By Juda and Jerusalem, according to the interpretation, each one’s soul can be understood, from which the Lord takes away all the things spoken of, either at the consummation of the world or at the end of each one, when it seemed to confess God and to have had the sense of peace. From such a Jerusalem God will destroy all pride, and false worship of God, and the errors of various doctrines, and the soul that serves the world and God alike, and the turning away from the Lord and the neglect of God through daily sins.
• Allegorically. When the charity of many shall grow cold and iniquity so abound that the Son of man at his coming will scarcely find faith on the earth, then God will strike those who seem to themselves to confess the name of the Lord, and the Church, which has its name from peace; and he will take away Baalim, which is interpreted “in the higher places”, that is, he will remove the vainglory that dwells in the Church, and the names of those who glory in being called bishops and priests by name alone; and “them that worship the host of heaven upon the tops of houses”, who lift themselves up against the knowledge of God, referring whatever is done in the world to the risings and settings of the stars; and those who worship the Lord and Melchom, who wish to please two masters at once, God and the world, who, having lost God their king, have the world and man for their king; and those who by evil works turn aside from the Lord’s rule, and do not seek him through penance.
1.5:
**“And them that worship the host of heaven upon the tops of houses”** — the sun and the moon and the other stars
**“and them that adore, and swear”** — at the same time
**“by the Lord, and swear by Melchom”**
• the idol of the Ammonites; and those too I will destroy
• Melchom: the idol of the Ammonites, said to be interpreted “king”.
1.6: **“And them that turn away from following after the Lord, and that have not sought the Lord, nor searched after him”** — They turn away from following after the Lord who, leaving his worship, swear by Melchom and worship the host of heaven.
1.7:
**“Be silent”** — Fear
**“before the face of the Lord God”** — from the captivity that hangs over you
**“Be silent before the face”** — Having now prophesied the captivity, he commands silence on all, striking a greater fear from the nearness of the captivity itself.
**“for … is near”** — the captivity prophesied under Josias is near
**“the day of the Lord”** — of captivity and of vengeance
**“for the Lord hath prepared”** — the overthrow of Jerusalem
**“a victim, he hath sanctified his guests”**
• that those he has devoted to death may be offered to him, as if to say: this victim pleases me
• Tropologically. All time is short compared with eternity, or each one’s end comes quickly. So he says: Let all fear, lest God’s angry face punish them either at each one’s end or at the common judgement; and if you will be just, you need not fear, for the Lord has prepared, in the Old Testament figurative victims for a remedy, and in the New the blood of Christ, the cleanser of all, through which those called from eternity are saved and sanctified; or through the blood of Christ the apostles are sanctified, and the others who were called through them.
• It can be said that he sanctified the Babylonians for vengeance on the sinning people, as avengers of the wrong done to God.
1.8:
**“And it shall come to pass in the day of the victim of the Lord”** — the day of the Jewish captivity, when the whole people is to be sacrificed
**“that I will visit upon the princes”** — who drank strong drink in the morning
**“and upon the king’s sons”** — either all of the royal stock, or properly the sons of Josias
**“and upon all such as are clothed with strange apparel”** — who instead of the worship of God worshipped idols
**“And it shall come to pass in the day of the victim”** — Mystically. In the day of the victim of his Son God will visit upon the high priests of the Jews and upon the royal house, for until that time there were kings of David’s line, but after this victim they failed, because they were clothed with strange apparel: they drew back from God’s protection and clothing, covered by their own error. These things can be taken of the day of judgement, in which the Lord will punish the princes who eat the milk and care nothing for the safety of the flock, and those who boast that they are the sons of Christ the king, and those who are clothed not with Christ but with the garment of the old man, that is, with vices, and through this have cast themselves out of the Church, handed over to Satan, and all who defile the Church with crimes. These things can also be understood of each one’s soul, whose sense and thought ought to be a lodging for God the king, but which clothes itself with the garments of various vices and fills the temple of its body with iniquity and deceit.
1.9:
**“And I will visit … upon every one that … arrogantly”** — the proud, who with a certain disdain and the haughtiness of rank go up the steps of the temple and the threshold of the sanctuary
**“in that day … entereth … over the threshold”** — THE SEPTUAGINT: Those who are in the porches, that is, those who have gone out of the Church because of their sins.
**“entereth … over the threshold”** — According to the Hebrew truth: they that leap over the threshold; which, historically, means: I will punish those who, according to the book of Kings, do not tread on the threshold, serving the superstitions of idols.
**“them that fill the house of the Lord their God with iniquity and deceit”** — they fill the house of God not only with the worship of idols but with every kind of their own iniquity, and with deceit to beguile those under them
1.10:
**“And there shall be in that day”**
• when, God’s hand stretched out over Jerusalem, the enemy army shall have besieged it
• The Fish Gate is the name of the gate that leads to Diospolis and Joppe, and it is nearer the sea than the Second; this means the gate of the second wall in the same quarter, from the hills of mount Sion and the higher part of the city: once that is taken by the enemy, the way down to the lower parts will be easier. Many refer these things to the times of the Babylonians.
**“saith the Lord, the noise of a cry”** — because of the cry of those who said “his blood be upon us and upon our children”, Jerusalem was besieged by the Romans; the captivity by Nabuchodonosor had gone before as a type of this captivity
**“and a howling from the Second, and a great destruction from the hills”**
• The first gate is that of the eyes, which are opened to covetousness. So in the judgement, when the books are opened, the whole image of their old crimes will be displayed before their eyes. After the cry of this gate follows the howling of the second, that is, of the ears. In these two senses man sins most and will be punished; seeing and hearing the whole train of his evils, whatever was lofty in man will be broken by this terror.
• Or, at the end of the world, those who did not keep their baptism will mourn from the first gate, the fish gate; from the second, those who did not do penance for their sins; and then they will be broken, because they would not be humbled. Through these two gates one enters, or returns, to the Church.
1.11:
**“Howl, ye inhabitants of the Morter”** — Morter: a hollow vessel in which grain is pounded, and fit for the use of physicians.
**“All the people of Chanaan is hush, all are cut off that were wrapped up in silver”**
• they shall perish who have such riches that they think themselves clothed and fenced about with them
• Howl, ye inhabitants: having described the cry that will be at the upper gate of the city, he adds also of the valley of Siloe, which he compares to a mortar, that is, a vessel in which grain is pounded, because the army rushing down from the fish gate and the Second and the hills will pound the lower places. He calls the people of the Jews Chanaan. Whence: “O thou seed of Chanaan, and not of Juda.”
• Howl. Those sunk in the depths of their crimes are called to lament. What is said, “All the people of Chanaan is hush”, means that in the day of judgement the blasphemy of those who have set their mouth against heaven will cease. Chanaan means “commotion”: by this name the Jews are called, whose feet were never fixed upon the rock.
1.12:
**“And it shall come to pass at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and will visit upon the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their hearts: The Lord will not do good, nor will he do evil”**
• trusting in their own strength, which is compared to lees, or to sins
• they slander God’s providence, saying that he can render neither good to the good nor evil to the evil, but all things are ruled by chance
• And it shall come to pass at that time: of the captivity by the Babylonians or the Romans, when no sin of those who forsook the law of God will remain unpunished, because no one will remain hidden, neither in the sewers nor in the caves in which kings and priests hid themselves for fear of death.
• I will search Jerusalem: at the time of judgement God will search his Church with a lamp, and will punish the despisers of his commandments, who, saying they sin as if with reason, blaspheme God, saying he can render neither rewards nor punishments; and to those sunk in blindness he will bring the lamp of his word and of reason, because he will bring all vices into the open.
• That say. In the day of judgement, or at each one’s death, what was raised up wickedly against God will be laid waste, so that the members they did not use well before may cease from evil work, and the houses they built in blood will be destroyed, and they will dwell not in a leprous house but in one well built; and because they planted the vineyard of Sodom and not of God, they will not drink its wine to be made drunk with Joseph at noon. For these the day of the Lord is near, compared with eternity, or because each one’s death makes the consummation of the world for him.
1.13:
**“And their strength shall become a booty, and their houses as a desert”** — If anyone plunders the strength of a robber or thief or pirate by making them weak, their weakness profits them
**“and they shall build houses”** — unclean, and therefore they will not dwell in them
**“and shall not dwell in them: and they shall plant vineyards”** — of Sodom
**“and shall not drink the wine of them”** — In both captivities the army of the Jews was cut down, their houses were pulled down, their fields and vineyards laid waste; and when they said to the prophets, “What you threaten will come to pass after a long time”, the Lord struck them quickly with a swift blow.
1.14:
**“The … day of the Lord is near”**
• which no one can withstand
• At the consummation of the world, or at each one’s end, the day of the Lord will be bitter for those who were wickedly mighty, when even the just are saved by fire; a day of misery, when they will say: woe to us, for we are wretched; a day of darkness, because darkness will follow those who hated the light; a day of clouds and whirlwind: God’s tempest will come upon them, whence God’s last trumpet will also terrify them; upon the cities which they fortified with a multitude of sins, and upon the corners, that is, perverse works, God’s anger will be raised. Whence the Pharisees too are rebuked, who pray at the corners of the streets, turning aside from the way of God, which is narrow and straight, and following crooked corners.
• The day of both captivities is bitter, because they provoked God to bitterness; and therefore not only the weak but the strongest men will be brought down, and those who spurned God’s light will be wrapped in darkness, and those who would not hear the trumpets of the solemn days will hear the trumpets of men at war. Of the destruction of the fenced cities and high corners of Judea, more can be learnt by the eyes than from writings.
1.16:
**“A day of the trumpet and alarm”** — there shall be
**“against the fenced cities, and against the high bulwarks”** — where there are scarcely small traces of the ruins
1.17:
**“And I will distress men”** — for the Lord’s cross Jerusalem suffered these evils
**“and they shall walk like blind men”**
• for the greatness of the pressure they will not know what to do
• and this is
**“because they have sinned against the Lord”** — first by shedding the blood of the prophets, afterwards of Christ; and therefore their blood shall be poured out over the whole region
**“and their blood shall be poured out as earth”** — as cheaply as dust
**“and their bodies as dung”**
• unburied upon the face of the land
• And I will distress men. At the end of the world, or of each one, those will be distressed who lived as men and died as men; and those who lost the light of virtues will go like blind men, not finding the light of penance. They have sinned against the Lord when, forsaking justice and the other virtues which are God’s, they followed injustice and the other vices. Their blood shall be poured out: by blood is understood the living soul by which a man is quickened and sustained and lives; whoever pours it out, whether by scandal or by perverse teaching, will have it poured out from him in the judgement, and will be forced to lose what seemed to him to be his life. For it would seem absurd if he said that anyone’s blood is to be poured out at the resurrection. So at the consummation, whether general or particular, the blood that was shed will cry to God, and will appear in the midst; and the works of blood and the earthly things will lie like dust and dung; and in that day in which the rich are forced by necessity to lose their riches, they will not be able to be delivered by them, because all earthly things will be devoured by God’s zeal.
• The rich who gathered riches with great iniquity will not be able to be delivered by them, because the fire of God’s zeal, kindled against them, will devour the whole land; not for a long time in the midst, for after forty-two years the destruction came, not only in Jerusalem, but on all who dwelt in the land of Judea.
• When God punishes out of zeal he shows that he loves the human soul; for unless he loved it he would not be jealous over it, nor, in the likeness of a husband, would he avenge his wife’s sin.
1.18: **“Neither shall their silver and their gold be able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the Lord: all the land shall be devoured by the fire of his jealousy, for he shall make even a speedy destruction of all them that dwell in the land”** — who have given themselves wholly to earthly things, and are not strangers and pilgrims in the world

2.1:
**“Assemble yourselves together”** — into one place, into one will, joined by the same charity
**“be gathered together, O nation not worthy to be loved”**
• not worthy of God’s love
• See God’s clemency: after the threat he calls them to penance, so that he need not do what he has threatened.
• Allegorically. It is said to the multitude of believers: Assemble in the Church, be joined in charity and peace, O nations who do not please God, since his discipline and commandments do not please you; but do penance before the day of judgement comes by God’s command. In it the wicked will be like dust passing away; at that time there will be no room for repenting, but only for receiving what God in his anger has brought. These things can also be applied to each one passing out of this world.
**“Assemble yourselves together, be gathered together”** — After describing the evils to come in both captivities, the people is called to penance.
2.2: **“Before the decree bring forth the day as dust passing away, before the fierce anger of the Lord come upon you”** — Before what has been prophesied is fulfilled, before God’s command prepares for itself a day on which the effect of the command follows, which will come as easily as dust passing away
2.3:
**“Seek the Lord”**
• O keepers of my commandments, who in imitation of me have been humbled in the world, who have wrought God’s judgement in meekness, seek the just one, to whom the Father has given all judgement; seek the meek one, so that whatever is lacking in your meekness may be filled up by him who is the fount of meekness.
• Allegorically. Let the meek of the Church seek the Lord, so that at the consummation of the world, or at each one’s end, they may be protected against God’s anger; for different evil men will be punished with different evils. This is what Gaza means, which is called “its strength”: that is, all who glory in strength of body will be brought to nothing in the day of God’s anger. Ascalon, that is, “weighed”, or “murderous fire”, will feel in God’s anger the measure of its crime, and because it burned to shed blood it will not be plundered like Gaza, but reduced to a desert will be burned to dust by the fires of Gehenna. And Azotus, that is, “fire of generations”, namely those who burn with lust and the fire of begetting, will be cast into darkness not by a hidden judgement but at noonday, when the saints will receive their full brightness. And Accaron, that is, “barrenness” or “rooting out”, namely those who bear no fruit but root out very many by perverse teaching: they too will be rooted out.
**“seek the just, seek the meek: if by any means you may be hid in the day of the Lord’s indignation”** — This is so that in some way you, the meek and the just, may escape the captivity to be brought on the Jews by Nabuchodonosor, or by the Romans, which will be so great that it will crush the mightiest cities of the Philistines along with you.
2.4:
**“For Gaza shall be destroyed, and Ascalon shall be a desert, they shall cast out Azotus at noonday”** — they will drag them into captivity not by stealth but in the open light
**“and Accaron shall be rooted up”** — it will suffer what its name sounds; for it is interpreted “rooting out”
2.5:
**“Woe to you that inhabit the sea coast”** — whose possession stretches along the sea
**“O nation of reprobates”** — given over to perdition
**“the word of the Lord upon you”**
• O
• a threat
**“O Chanaan”** — namely
**“the land of the Philistines”** — no one doubts that the land of the Philistines is the land of Chanaan
**“Woe to you that inhabit”**
• Having foretold the laying waste of four great cities of Palestine, the word is directed to the province itself in general, and foretells to them: woe at the coming of the Babylonians, for even those who dwell by the sea will be taken away by them.
• Tropologically. Either at the consummation of the world, or daily through churchmen, God’s threat is made to correct those who, when they ought to dwell in Judea, that is, the land of promise or of confession, prefer to dwell in the sea and be beaten by the waves of the world; and they are also called the land of Chanaan, ever in motion, and Philistines, falling by the cup. God destroys these from their former dwelling, so that the region that once held a lost flock may begin to be the fold of Christ’s sheep, and Juda, that is, true confession, may dwell on the sea coast; and when the evening of the world comes, of the many called the few chosen, who are now called the remnant of the house of Juda, will feed those who once fed in the sea and who were once in Ascalon, that is, in whom the gore of the slain once flowed, for Ascalon is called “murderous fire”. And this is because God has visited his people, and will lead back to the knowledge of the truth those who were easily deceived by the sophistries of heretics, and make them victors over their enemies.

• Allegorically. By the children of Ammon and Moab the Jews and the heretics are signified; for they too seem to be of Abraham’s stock and to have escaped the burning of Sodom and Gomorrha and to dwell in little Segor. But because their generation is in darkness, and they are sons of Lot, that is, turning aside from God, and born of incestuous unions, therefore, insulting the sons of Juda, that is, the true confessors, over their possession, they long to magnify their own borders. For trusting in the subtlety of sophistries they despise the Church’s plainness as unworthy of their mysteries, which they have fashioned for themselves like idols. Therefore they will be like Sodom and Gomorrha. They seem indeed, in that they are not Gentiles, to have come out of Sodom; but because they blaspheme, they slip back into Sodom, and are thorns prepared for the burning by the dryness of their vices. They are also, by the multitude of their vices, a heap of salt that has lost its savour. So those who would not possess the land of the Church will be left desolate for ever.

1.1:
**“In the second year of Darius the king”**
• When Cyrus king of the Persians, Baltasar having been slain, had taken the kingdom of the Babylonians with Darius his uncle, king of the Medes, in the first year of his reign he sent back to Jerusalem about fifty thousand Jews, over whom he set Zorobabel and Jesus the son of Josedec, and commanded them to rebuild the temple of the Lord. They built the altar and laid the foundations of the temple. But meanwhile Cyrus died, and Artaxerxes, succeeding him, ordered the nations round about Jerusalem not to allow the temple to be rebuilt. So the work remained unfinished until the second year of Darius son of Hystaspes. In this year the prophets Aggeus and Zacharias, fearing neither the king’s edict nor the enmity of the surrounding peoples, exhorted Zorobabel and the people with him to rebuild the temple, because the time had now come in which Jeremias had prophesied that the temple was to be rebuilt. And Zorobabel and the people obeyed the prophets who exhorted them rather than the king or the peoples who forbade them.
• Darius is interpreted “generations”, and signifies a lover of intercourse and of fleshly begetting. Fittingly, then, this vision is seen by the people in the time of Darius, a people that, returned from captivity, had not yet built the temple nor had the glory of the former Jerusalem, but dwelt in hollow, low-lying houses. Rightly too is it seen in the second year, because two is an unclean number, which, first departing from the virginity of unity, is the beginning of all alternation. Whence in Genesis it is not said after the works of the second day were finished, as is added after the works of the other days: and God saw that it was good. The sixth month too is fitting, because this month has no solemnities of God, as the seventh has, but is like the six days in which the world was made, in which one labours and eats bread in the sweat of the brow. But because the altar had already been built, the word comes on one day, that the people, forsaking the shrine of Darius and the sixth month, may return to the unity of faith.
**“in the sixth month, in the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came”**
• God inspires a prophet who has good works, that through him the prince of the people may be taught
• seeking to whom he might come and whom he might teach
**“by the hand of Aggeus the prophet”** — Aggeus is “festive”, by whose hand the word of God comes. So everyone who keeps God’s feasts with the unleavened bread of sincerity can receive the word of God. The word of God does not come to those who killed the Word, that is, the Son of God, because their hands are full of blood.
**“to Zorobabel”**
• who was born in Babylon, as Christ in the confusion of the world
• Zorobabel is a type of the Saviour, who builds for the Father the tabernacle that was destroyed, both from the remnant of the Jews and from the multitude of the Gentiles. Zo- “this”, ro- “master”, -babel, that is, of Babylon: that is, this master of Babylon, who was born in Babylon, leads the people back from Babylon into the land of promise from which they had been carried away captive. Or Zorobabel is “an outpouring set forth”: this is the outpouring of Jesus, which is set forth for us from the most abundant fountain to be drawn upon. Whence he himself says: If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink. This fountain we receive by devout petitions. Whence Zorobabel is the son of Salathiel, which is interpreted “petition of God”.
**“the son of Salathiel, governor of Juda”** — because he was of the stock of David
**“and to Jesus the son of Josedec the high priest”**
• in these two one Christ is signified, king and high priest
• who was of the priestly tribe
• Josedec is “the Lord is just”, that is, God the Father, whose son is Jesus, that is, the Saviour, compared with whom all priests are found least.
1.2:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts, saying: This people saith: The time is not yet come for building the house of the Lord”**
• not Zorobabel, not Jesus, but the people says it, which does not yet refuse the yoke of servitude under Darius
• This people saith. Those who are held captive outside Jerusalem put off building the temple of the Lord, and say: the time is not yet come for building the house of the Lord.
• When someone who has gone out of the Church through vice resolves to rebuild God’s temple in himself, and yet puts it off from day to day, it can be said of him: This man says, it is not yet the time for building the house of God. But every time is fitting for building, and enemies cannot hinder him who has turned to God and cried out.
1.3: **“And the word of the Lord came by the hand of Aggeus the prophet, saying”** — And the word came. On the same day as above this vision is seen again; and as the prophet’s works advance, the gifts of prophecy too increase; and after a little silence, it is as if the Lord’s answer were a considered one.
1.4:
**“Is it time for you to dwell in ceiled houses”** — the Septuagint: hollow
**“Is it time”** — Is it then time for you to dwell in houses set in the valley, while my house, which is on the mountain, lies desolate? Or to dwell in ceiled houses, that is, adorned and luxurious, while the holy of holies lies open to the rains and to every injury?
**“and this house lie desolate?”** — All the time in which we choose to dwell in the valley, that is, in vices and the luxury of the world, is counted as nothing, and God finds no place in us to lay his head.
1.5:
**“And now thus saith the Lord of hosts”** — whose command is no light thing
**“Set your hearts”**
• which until now were drawn away by divers ways
• Do nothing without counsel and forethought, but let the light of the divine law shine before your feet.
**“to consider your ways”**
• call to mind what you have done and what you have suffered
• Turn my commandments into deeds without delay
1.6:
**“You have sowed much, and brought in”** — into the barns
**“little”** — you received less than you sowed
**“but have not had enough”** — because you had small harvests
**“you have drunk, but have not been filled with drink”**
• made merry
• lest anyone say the fast had been willing
**“you have clothed yourselves, but have not been warmed”** — you had a cloak, but one that neither kept out the cold nor kept in the warmth
**“and he that hath earned wages, put them into a bag with holes”**
• If anyone has gathered wages, whether by trade or by hired labour, his money runs away as if it were put into a bag with holes
• You have sowed much. The famine did not come because the farmer had left off farming.
• Mystically. Those who have returned from Babylon and put off building the house of God, saying, It is not yet the time for building the house of the Lord, are neither captives nor fully free, but placed as it were in the middle: they sow and reap little; for if among many sins they do some just works, God is not unjust, to forget the few good things because of the many evil, but he will make him reap and gather into barns what he sowed in good ground. He who does nothing at all eats nothing, but perishes of hunger. He who sows much and brings in little will eat little, not to the full nor with sweetness. But the holy man will eat to the full.
**“you have clothed yourselves”** — He who has a cloak, that is, the hidden knowledge of God’s mysteries woven of senses and words, does not let those fervent in spirit lose the warmth of love and suffer cold. He who is not so fervent has indeed the cloak of his senses and works, but is not warmed, nor wholly covered. And he who for the poverty of his soul has no cloak, because through multiplied iniquity charity has grown cold in him, therefore perishes of cold.
**“he that hath earned wages”** — He who works good things worthy of reward, and does not cease to add good to good, puts his wages into a bag without holes. But he who fouls his former good deeds with vices that follow gathers into a bag with holes.
1.7:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts: Set Your hearts upon your ways”**
• the same Lord urges the same thing as before
• Set your hearts. The Hebrews falsely say that only timber was needed for the gathering, since the walls of the temple were standing after the burning.
• Mystically. After our hearts have been set upon our ways, we are commanded to go up to the mountain, that is, to the height of the divine word, that from it we may cut for ourselves timber, that is, testimonies and various kinds of virtues, to build in ourselves the house of wisdom, that it may please God and he may be glorified in us.
• Consider all that you do, and leaving the care of your own lowly houses, go up to the mountain where there is wood that will not be burned but will serve the works of my house; and that you may do this the more gladly, know that in this you will please me.
1.9:
**“You have looked for more”** — Often much good is hoped for from many whose teaching and conduct seem good. But when the time of harvest comes, that is, when they have the time for teaching and get the opportunity of instructing others by the example of their life, little or nothing is found in them; and as negligence creeps in little by little they lose even the little they seemed to have. This befalls them because they were secure in their former houses, and did not go up the mountain of the Scriptures, nor build up the house of the Lord in themselves.
**“and you brought it home”** — See another hardship that befell those who put off the building: when at harvest time they thought they held the grain in their hands, they were gathering empty husks without fruit; and the little that was left over they brought into the house, but the power of God blew it away, that is, brought it to nothing, because the husks were empty and the empty grain had no flour.
**“why”** — these evils befall you
**“saith the Lord of hosts”** — and you each dwell in your own house
**“because my house is desolate, and you make haste”** — otherwise: you have made haste
1.10:
**“from giving dew”** — Mystically. Dew is the blessing of heavenly grace, which comes down not from the air, where there are many disturbances, but from heaven, to water souls wounded by the devil’s dart, or burning in persecution.
**“and the earth was hindered from yielding her fruits”**
• they give not only no rain, but not even the night’s dew, so that the fields might at least be tempered with a little moisture
• what it is wont to bring forth of itself, it holds back in its greedy lap once it is entrusted to it
• Mystically. A sword, or a burning wind, is the word of God, sharper than any sword, which destroys the dry land, that is, the negligent soul that dwells in hollow places, so that it bears no fruit. It is called down upon the mountains too, those that lift themselves up against the knowledge of God; it destroys also the wheat and the wine and the oil with which, as with food and drink, heretics coax the peoples they have deceived: their bread is the bread of sorrow, their wine the gall of dragons, their oil that which fattens the sinner’s head. By men are meant their senses and thoughts, or by men the learned, by beasts the unlearned, who perish with the works of their hands, that is, with fasts and various observances. These things can be understood of the wicked teachers of the Church, who, seeking fleshly things, do not seek to rebuild the ruined house of God either in themselves or in others, but scandalize many by word and example.
1.11:
**“And I called for a drought”**
• or: a sword; better: a burning wind
• Whatever heretics invent of their own accord without the authority of scripture, as if it were apostolic tradition, God’s sword strikes.
**“and upon the mountains, and upon the corn, and upon the wine, and upon the oil, and upon all that the ground bringeth forth, and upon men, and upon beasts, and upon all the labour of the hands”**
• drought is called upon the mountains, that they may not bring forth wheat, wine and oil, or whatever the ground brings forth of itself
• famine going before, death follows upon men and beasts
• the same burning wind consumes all that men’s hands have laboured at
1.12:
**“Then Zorobabel the son of Salathiel, and Jesus the son of Josedec the high priest, and all the remnant of the people hearkened”**
• otherwise: the rest
• who did not come to the perfect man
**“to the voice of the Lord their God, and to the words of Aggeus the prophet, as the Lord their God sent him to them: and the people feared before the Lord”**
• knowing that the face of the Lord is “against them that do evil things: to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth”
• Those who have come to the perfect man hear, obey, and do not fear, for “charity casteth out fear”.
**“hearkened”** — By Zorobabel and Jesus one Christ is signified, king and priest; and so they do not fear, but only the people fears.
1.13:
**“And Aggeus the messenger of the Lord … spoke”** — Some think that John the Baptist, and Malachias, which is interpreted “angel of the Lord”, and Aggeus were angels, and that for the dispensation they took human bodies at God’s command and lived among men. Whence they say that John the Baptist leapt in his mother’s womb at Mary’s voice. But we say that the prophet is called God’s messenger, that is, angel, which in Hebrew is “malachi”, because he announces God’s will to men.
**“I am with you”** — I will be your helper: build my house, which is destroyed in you; set me in your midst; no one will be able to hinder your building.
**“saith the Lord”**
• one of the messengers, a prophet of the prophets
• He does not speak to Zorobabel, or Jesus, with whom and in whom he always was, but to the fearful people, which received as the reward for its fear of God that the Lord should be with them
1.14:
**“And the Lord stirred up”**
• as if it had been asleep before
• Now the true Zorobabel of the stock of David and Jesus, priest for ever, has been raised up by the Father’s power; with his help we must be stirred up to build the spiritual house of God, and entering it we must offer spiritual sacrifices and do works worthy of God’s temple, which yet we cannot do unless we have first feared the Lord. But because we are in the world, and build while serving generation and marriage under Darius, we therefore enter the house of God in the sixth number, in which the world was made, and in the second year, which is divided from unity. And since the world was made in six, six must be doubled for the world to be remade; and so in twelve is the restoring of the human race; and to show that it is made of both peoples, we double twelve; and so on the twenty-fourth day the Church was built, both from the Gentiles and from the circumcision. Or eight refers to circumcision, three to faith in the Trinity: through faith in the Trinity comes the true circumcision of vices. So, eight being multiplied by three, on the twenty-fourth day we build the house.
**“the spirit of Zorobabel the son of Salathiel governor of Juda, and the spirit of Jesus the son of Josedec the high priest, and the spirit of all the rest of the people: and they went in”** — for they had been outside
**“and did the work”** — which was worthy of the inner rooms of the house of God
**“in the house of the Lord of hosts their God”**
• not the body, not the soul, but the spirit, which knows better how to build a temple for the Lord
• that the kingdom and the priesthood might build a temple for God
1.15: **“In the four and twentieth day”** — The same year of Darius, and the same month as was set at the beginning, but not the same day. For there it says “in the first day of the month”, here “in the four and twentieth”, so that between the first day, on which the Lord speaks through Aggeus, and the twenty-fourth, on which they went in, there were twenty-two days between, in which the people feared the Lord.

2.1:
**“And in the seventh month, the word of the Lord came”** — by working he deserved that the word of God should come to him more fully
**“And in the seventh month”** — The same year, but in the seventh month, in which are the solemnities of God, on the twenty-first day of the month, that is, when three weeks are completed and rest made perfect in the mystery of the Trinity, the word of God comes a third time to Aggeus, who always laboured to this end, that the word of the Lord might come to him.
**“by the hand of Aggeus the prophet, saying”** — The word of God comes to those who had begun to work in the house of God, now in rest, that is, in the seventh month, and in the full sacrament of the Trinity, that is, on the twenty-first of the month; to Aggeus, who keeps God’s feasts; to Zorobabel son of Salathiel, who deigned to become man for us, and priest; and to the rest of the people: compared with the whole world, the believers were a small part at the beginning. Who is left among you? Judea was once the house of God, serving the one God according to the precepts of the law, and beloved in the fathers Abraham, David and the rest; but now, blinded, it has begun to be not beloved, nor the people of God. This house in the sight of Christ and of the believing people is counted as though it were not. So Christ is called on to strengthen his kingdom and priesthood. And the people too who dwelt in the hollows of earthly things is called to do spiritual work in the house of God, and to know that God is present to them and works spiritually in them what he once covenanted in figure with those coming out of Egypt. He promises too his spirit as helper to those who work in his house and fulfil the word of his covenant. I moved the heaven when my voice was heard from heaven, and the earth when I gave the testament to the former people, and at my coming, mist, whirlwind and darkness were seen. I moved the sea when I gave a way to the people passing over. I moved the dry land, that is, Egypt, by the plagues, since it was empty of the worship of God; or the wilderness, which the people went round for forty years. And I who did these things in the giving of the old law will yet move the heaven and the earth at the time of the passion: the heaven, when the sun was darkened and there was darkness; the earth, when the rocks were split and the tombs opened; the sea, when the dragon that was in it was slain; the dry land, the fruitless multitude of the Gentiles; and when these are moved I will move all nations to the faith, for his sound went out into all the earth. And this will be when the desired of all nations comes, at whose coming the Church will be filled with a greater glory than there was in the synagogue, as Christ the Son is greater in the Church than Moses the servant in the synagogue; and this glory will be given through silver, that is, the words of the Scriptures, and gold, that is, the hidden sense that dwells in the hearts of the saints.
2.2: **“Speak to Zorobabel the son of Salathiel the governor of Juda, and to Jesus the son of Josedec the high priest, and to the rest of the people”** — who saw the old house of God and are now present at its restoration
2.3:
**“Who is left among you, that saw this house in its first glory? and how do you see it now?”** — as nothing in comparison with the former
**“Who is left among you”** — There was once in Israel a house of God, which was now so desolate that in the sight of those who saw it it was counted as though it had not been; which is to be taken not only of the buildings of the temple, but of everything that the Jews once had that was glorious.
2.4:
**“Yet now take courage, O Zorobabel”** — but do not despair
**“saith the Lord, and take courage, O Jesus the son of Josedec the high priest, and take courage, all ye people of the land, saith the Lord of hosts: and perform”** — the work in my house
**“for I”** — the Father
2.5:
**“The word”** — the Son
**“that I covenanted with you when you came out”** — otherwise: when you came out
**“of the land of Egypt: and … spirit”** — Holy
**“my … shall be in the midst of you”** — there hath stood one in the midst of you, whom you know not
**“fear not”** — I who command am almighty, for whom to say is to do
2.6:
**“For thus saith the Lord of hosts: Yet one little while, and I will move the heaven and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land”**
• at the time of the passion the sun was darkened
• And I will move the heaven and the earth. When I gave the first Testament on Sinai, I moved the heaven and the earth and the Red Sea and the wilderness, to make a testament with you; but now I promise that I will yet move the heaven and the earth, so that when they are moved all nations may be moved, and then the desired of all nations will come, that is, the Saviour, and then I will fill this house with a greater glory than before.
2.7:
**“And I will move all nations”** — the opposing powers, unable to bear the splendour of the Lord
**“AND THE DESIRED OF ALL NATIONS SHALL COME: and I will fill this house with glory: saith the Lord of hosts”** — lest you think the one who makes the promise weak
2.8: **“The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the Lord of hosts”** — that is, all the riches that I will give you for the adorning of the temple, so that the glory of this house may be greater than that of the former
2.9:
**“Great shall be the glory of this last house more than of the first, saith the Lord of hosts: and in this place I will give peace”** — which surpasseth all understanding
**“and in this place I will give”** — Because nothing avails so much for the building of a glorious house as peace, I promise that peace shall be given in this place, so that my place may be in the peace which surpasseth all understanding.
2.10:
**“In the four and twentieth day”**
• as above
• Multiply twenty by four and it will be eighty, a number that has forty twice. Forty signifies penance, which ought to be not only of the body but also of the spirit, which eighty shows.
**“of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius”** — as above
**“of the ninth month”** — This number is never taken in a good sense. Every solemnity ends on the eighth day and does not reach the ninth. Jerusalem in Jeremias is taken by the Babylonians in the ninth month. So, because the prophecy was to be about the people’s uncleanness, the ninth month is joined to the second year of Darius; but because room is given for penance after the uncleanness is corrected, the word of the Lord comes to Aggeus on the twenty-fourth day, that, as if in the person of the Lord, he may put to the priests a question coming from the law.
**“the word of the Lord came to Aggeus the prophet, saying”** — To Aggeus the prophet, not “by the hand of Aggeus”, as above. For there he had progress, and only clean works, but his heart had not yet received full wisdom. Or because he still dwelt among those who said: The time is not yet come for building the house of the Lord. The word of the Lord came only in his works. But now the foundations of the temple have been laid, and the people, having gone in with the princes, does the work of God and hears the mysteries. “I will move all nations”: he is full of prophecy, and so the word comes to the whole Aggeus.
2.11: **“Thus saith the Lord of hosts: Ask the priests the law, saying”** — It is the priest’s part to know the law of the Lord and to answer the Lord’s question about the law: if he is a priest, let him know the law of the Lord; if he does not know the law, he proves himself not to be a priest of the Lord.
2.12:
**“If a man carry sanctified flesh in the skirt of his garment, and touch with his skirt, bread, or pottage”** — any cooked food for eating
**“or wine, or oil, or any meat: shall it be sanctified? And the priests answered, and said: No”**
• it shall be sanctified; but each thing stays as it was
• Anagogically. The churchman who sacrifices the spotless lamb and has put on Christ ties holy flesh in his cloak when he sets out to instruct his hearers about the outward sacraments; and with this cloak he touches, by expounding, the divine scripture, which is bread that strengthens man’s heart, and is pottage, that is, a cooked dish, as are the apostolic feasts, which season and cook the flesh of the old law and offer it seasoned for eating; scripture is also wine that gladdens man’s heart, it is also oil that makes the face cheerful, it is also the food of milk by which little ones are nourished, and other such things. But while the hearers are taught through scripture about the outward sacraments, they do not eat it as sanctified food, because they are not refreshed within by the inner richness of the sacraments. On the other hand the author of perverse teaching makes unclean whomever he infects with his teaching. For the wicked too have bread in their teaching, but of mourning; and wine, but of mad drunkenness; and the oil of flattery; they have pottage too, when, to confirm their perversity, they mix in mystical things from the scriptures as a seasoning; they have other foods too, that is, various treatises, which, because they were written by the unclean and uttered by an unclean mouth, make whoever touches them unclean, and he will be led into their error.
**“If a man carry … flesh”** — The flesh offered on the altar was eaten sometimes by the priests in the hidden parts of the temple, sometimes by their kinsfolk at home, sometimes by those of the priests who were seen to be blemished, sometimes by Israelites who had no uncleanness. And he was called unclean who had touched a dead man. For as long as the soul is in the body, the human body is not unclean, but as soon as the soul departs. So the prophet asks: if any man carries sanctified flesh, and ties it in the skirt of his garment, and the skirt touches bread, or anything a man can eat, can that food be sanctified by that touch? The answer is that it is not sanctified.
2.13:
**“And Aggeus said: If one that is unclean … touch”** — who has been made unclean by contact with a dead man
**“by occasion of a soul … any of all these things, shall it be defiled? And the priests answered”** — whose chief was Jesus, through whom they knew the law
**“and said: It shall be defiled”** — it is defiled by the touch of the defiled
**“If one that is unclean … touch”** — He puts another question, because they answered the first well, and in this one the unskilled can easily be caught: for it can seem that, just as it is not sanctified, so it is not defiled either.
2.14:
**“And Aggeus answered”** — who knows the differences of the solemnities, and so is called “festive”
**“and said: So is this people”** — which is unclean in soul: everything it touches and offers me will be unclean
**“and so is this nation”** — the Gentiles and the heretics
**“before my face, saith the Lord”** — though it seems holy to men in its outward show
**“and so is all the work of their hands”** — vows, prayers, fasting, almsgiving, even continence in the body
**“and all”** — the things spoken of above
**“that they have offered there, shall be defiled”**
• And Aggeus answered. Saying nothing of the first question, he weaves the occasion of his discourse from the second: So is this people.
• According to the letter: O people, who, while my house is still in ruins, offer victims on the altar already built, and think you are sanctified by that flesh, know that you are not so much sanctified by them as that all your works are defiled, because you strive to build your own house rather than mine; nor does the holy thing offered on the altar help you while you dwell in the valleys and are defiled by dead works.
2.15:
**“And now consider in your hearts”** — to consider
**“from this day and upward, before there was a stone laid upon a stone”** — consider also what was done before, what and how much you suffered, so that when prosperity comes afterwards you may know its cause by the contrast
**“in the temple of the Lord”**
• the twenty-fourth of the ninth month
• And now consider. As if to say: although these things you offered on the altar, while the temple was not yet built, are defiled, yet, O people, I urge you to turn your mind back to the past, to the great evils with which I afflicted you before you began to lay the foundations of the temple, so that when you have thought again on the evils you suffered for the destruction of the temple, you may afterwards set your heart to consider the good things you have begun to have from the first day of the building, and those that are to be given you more fully in the future, after the temple is fully built.
• Allegorically. You who have believed in Jesus, consider the time when in your heathendom you served vices and did not build in yourselves the temple whose foundation is Christ, on whom let each one see how he builds. Consider what you suffered before, when you went to a heap of twenty bushels: whatever virtues and good works you seemed to have before Christ were, beyond your hope, unfruitful, so that it could be said to you: Have you suffered so many things in vain? And when you expected fifty vessels from the vineyard, a number made perfect when seven weeks are completed with the oneness of the Godhead, and thought you had the wine that gladdens man’s heart, the sacred number thirty was taken away, the age at which Christ was baptized and at which the priests approach the mystery of God, and twenty is left: the number Jacob, seeing it loved by Esau, sent him animals by, twenty and twenty. Though among unbelievers there is no fruit of good works for eternity, yet they are said to receive half the reward of their labour, when, hoping for twenty, they find ten, that is, fruit and glory in the present time for the labour spent; and this is so that they may not wholly despair, but, turned at some time, may lay stone upon stone; otherwise they will lose even the half. Whence there follows: I struck you with a blasting wind: whatever is struck by blasting wind and mildew and hail is reduced to dust and ashes, and nothing useful is found in it; and this because they do not return to God. But those who return will be blessed by the Lord. Whence there follows: from this day I will bless, and so on.
2.16:
**“When you went”** — namely, consider this
**“to a heap of twenty bushels”** — where you thought there were twenty, you could scarcely gather half
**“and they became ten: and you went”** — the vines, to the eye, promised fifty vessels, but you had not even half
2.17:
**“I struck you with a blasting wind”** — others: with rust
**“and with the mildew”** — others: with blight
**“and with hail, all the works of your hand, yet there was none among you that returned to me, saith the Lord”**
• and I did this, striking you with a blasting wind and mildew, to rouse you by the weight of evils to the knowledge of me; but not even so would you return
• I struck you. In vain does anyone think he can appease God with alms and offerings when he has not built in himself a temple for the Holy Spirit.
2.18:
**“Set your hearts from this day”** — Consider what plenty there will be
**“and henceforward, from the four and twentieth day of the ninth month: from the day that the foundations … were laid”** — otherwise: laid
