**“Set your hearts”** — I have set out what you suffered before you began to build; now I will set out the good things that are to be given you after you have begun to build.
**“of the temple of the Lord … and lay it up in your hearts”**
• The ninth month from April, which is the first among the Hebrews, is December among us; in this month the seeds lie hidden in the earth, and the coming fruitfulness cannot be guessed.
• That the ninth month is not taken in a good sense the history tells in the books of Kings and of Jeremias, the month in which Jerusalem was besieged; yet because the foundations of the temple were laid at the end of the ninth month, we understand that the house of God is not built in us unless evil works first come to an end. But whoever has dedicated himself zealously to the worship of God does not know the measure of his harvest and his reward, because sowing in the Holy Spirit, he will reap of the Holy Spirit life everlasting.
2.19:
**“Is”** — as if to say: not
**“the seed as yet sprung up?”** — in this month the shoot is sent out from the grain
**“as yet”** — in this month
**“the vine, and the fig tree, and the pomegranate, and the olive tree … flourished?”** — so that from the flower the fruit may be known
**“Is the seed as yet”** — Do not say that I guess this by shrewd reasoning and suppose the coming plenty from the flowers of the trees and the blades of the crops, for in this month there are no signs; and yet I foretell to you, because you have begun to build my temple, the fruitfulness of all crops by my blessing.
**“from this day I will bless you”** — The vine is the word of the Lord, whose Father is the husbandman; the fig, the sweetest gifts of the Holy Spirit; the pomegranate, the Church’s teachings and the knowledge of the scriptures, all of which in the Canticle are compared to the bride’s cheeks; the olive tree gives refreshment and light to those who have begun to build the temple of God. In the vine the Saviour is understood, in the fig the Holy Spirit, in the olive the person of the Father. As we read in the book of Judges, where the fruitless trees ask the vine and the fig and the olive to reign over them, but they refuse rule over the fruitless. So those trees come to the bramble, a thorny shrub, which hurts and wounds whatever it touches as if with hooks, and consumes its subjects with its fire, that is, the devil, who reigns in the barren. The Father and the Son and the Spirit reign there where the pomegranate is: a tree which, for its great multitude of seeds and its various cells divided by interwoven skins, yet all held in one rind, is always set in the holy scriptures for the person of the Church.
2.20:
**“to Aggeus”** — Not “by the hand” as before, nor “to Aggeus the prophet” as in the fourth vision, but only “to Aggeus”, that is, one who keeps the feasts of the Lord, who announces and sees him not as one to come but as one coming. As Abraham saw the day of Christ and was glad, and John pointed out the Lamb of God with his finger, so Aggeus too, seeing the kingdom of the Son of God, has all the solemnities in himself.
**“And the word of the Lord came a second time to Aggeus in the four and twentieth day of the month, saying”** — The four and twentieth of the month. Note that it is on the same day, that is, the twenty-fourth of the ninth month, the number of the month being left unsaid, because it prophesies of Christ’s coming and of his kingdom.
2.21: **“Speak to”** — These things can be said of both comings, because Christ reigned when he came, and will reign when he comes. If we will take it of the end of the world, we shall say that all principality and all power and might is to be destroyed, that God may be all in all. Because what is said is mystical and belongs to the end of things, the prophet is bidden to speak to Zorobabel alone, who signifies Christ, who is of the seed of David: how the fashion of this world passes away, and he makes a new heaven and a new earth.
2.22:
**“And I will overthrow”** — when all eagerness for fighting is scattered, peace will follow
**“the throne of kingdoms”** — the seats of kings
**“and will destroy the strength of the kingdom of the Gentiles”** — the opposing kingdom, so that the destruction of their kingdom may profit even those who reigned before
**“and I will overthrow the chariot”** — principality, power, might
**“and him that rideth therein: and the horses and their riders shall come down”**
• so that this may be
• When the eagerness for war is ended there will be one fold and one shepherd: both hosts, as well of the Gentiles as of the Jews, will be held under the peaceful shepherd.
**“every one by the sword of his brother”** — that is, by the most sharp word of God he will rise against his brother, cutting off all that is contrary
2.23:
**“and will make thee”** — And when this has been fulfilled, I will set thee, O Christ, my Son, in my hand as a signet: him hath God the Father sealed, and he is the image of the invisible God, and the figure of his substance, so that whoever believes in God may be sealed with him as with a ring.
**“In that day, saith the Lord of hosts”** — behold the best end of all
**“I will take thee, O Zorobabel the son of Salathiel, my servant”** — Christ, the Father’s servant according to the flesh

1.1:
**“In the eighth month”**
• In the eighth month. Cyrus king of the Persians, who destroyed the empire of the Chaldeans, in the first year of his reign sent back about fifty thousand captives from Babylon into Judea, and returned the vessels that Nabuchodonosor had taken away, and commanded the temple to be rebuilt, and appointed Zorobabel and Jesus the high priest as princes of those returning. When Cyrus, who reigned thirty years in Persia, was killed among the Massagetae by Tamyris their queen, Cambyses son of Cyrus succeeded to the kingdom; when his eight years were completed, he had as successors two brothers, magi; and when they were killed by the people, Darius son of Hystaspes was made king of the Persians. In the second year of his reign the word of the Lord came to Zacharias son of Barachias son of Addo. So from the first year of Cyrus to the second year of Darius forty years are reckoned, in which only the altar had been built and the foundations of the temple laid, the neighbouring nations round about and Cambyses king of the Persians forbidding the work, as Esdras writes. So in the second year of Darius Aggeus and Zacharias began to exhort the people to the restoring of the temple, broken off for so long.
• November, which, the heat of summer being spent, is the beginning of winter, a time in which no solemnity is kept by the law. For there were three great solemnities: the first called the Pasch, the second Pentecost, the third the solemnity of Tabernacles in the month of September. So in the wintry month of November the prophet is sent to a people still weighed down by the cold of tribulations.
**“in the second year of king Darius … came”** — in Zacharias
**“the word of the Lord”** — which “was in the beginning with God”
**“to Zacharias”** — is interpreted “remembrance of the Lord”
**“the son of Barachias”** — is interpreted “blessing of the Lord”
**“the son of Addo, the prophet, saying”**
• mystically: for Addo is interpreted “his witness”
• Zacharias is “remembrance of the Lord”, Barachias “blessing of the Lord”, Addo “his witness”. Since the people, though hindered from building the temple, yet kept the remembrance of God, and for the remembrance had the blessing, and for the blessing the witness, therefore Zacharias son of Barachias son of Addo is sent to comfort the people.
**“Addo”** — He is Ananias, who was sent to Jeroboam son of Nabat, under whom the altar was overthrown, and his hand withered, and was restored again at his prayers.
1.2:
**“The Lord hath been exceeding angry with your fathers”**
• he punished those who would not be corrected by the prophets’ warnings
• who are not corrected
• The Lord hath been angry: God’s anger signifies not any disturbance in him, but the deserts and sins of those to be punished, who are punished by God so that they may be amended.
**“The Lord hath been … angry”** — God’s anger signifies not a disturbance in him, who is not angry, but the sins of those against whom he is severe; nor does he take vengeance in anger, but chastises in order to amend. Whence: “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation, nor chastise me in thy wrath”; and elsewhere: “Correct us, O Lord, but yet not in thy fury, but in mercy.”
1.3:
**“And”** — yet
**“thou shalt say to them”** — O Zacharias
**“Thus saith”** — though angry
**“the Lord of hosts”**
• not a man, not Zacharias
• who is to be feared
• in Hebrew: Sabaoth
**“Thus saith the Lord”** — Note that in Aggeus and Zacharias, in a few short verses and brief sentences, “saith the Lord of hosts” is always added, that they may know it is God who commands, and may be stirred by this confidence to build the temple against the king’s command and the enemies raging round about.
**“Turn ye to me”** — having returned from Babylon
**“Turn ye to”** — He commands that, returned from Babylon, they turn to God, and God will turn to them, so that the sons may not suffer what their fathers suffered for their sins.
**“saith the Lord of hosts: and I will turn to you, saith the Lord of hosts”** — Whence: draw near to the Lord and he will draw near to you. And on the other hand: you have departed from me, and I have departed from you.
1.4:
**“Be not as your fathers”** — like them in punishment if you are like them in guilt; as if to say: learn from the danger of others
**“to whom”** — to correct them
**“have cried”** — openly
**“the former prophets”** — for at that time there were Isaias, Osee, Joel and others
**“saying: Thus”** — namely this
**“saith the Lord of hosts”** — whom to resist is madness
**“Turn ye”** — to the Lord
**“from … ways”** — of your deeds
**“your evil … and from your wicked thoughts: but they did not give ear, neither did they hearken to me, saith the Lord”** — they despised not the prophets who spoke, but me who was in the prophets
1.5:
**“Your fathers, where are they?”** — who would not be converted
**“and the prophets, shall they live always?”** — the false prophets who deceived them
1.6:
**“But yet my words, and my ordinances, which I gave in charge to my servants the prophets, did they not take hold of your fathers, and they returned, and said: As the Lord of hosts thought to do to us according to our ways, and according to our devices”** — so
**“But yet my words”** — Both those who would not be converted and those who deceived with false promises are taken away by death, but the words I spoke through my prophets remain for ever; they took hold of your fathers and showed that what I said was true; and your fathers, proving in themselves by the outcome of events that my prophecies were true, repented and said: God has repaid us according to our works and our sins, and what we suffer has justly befallen us.
1.7:
**“In the four and twentieth day of the eleventh month which is called Sabath”**
• the third, namely after the eighth, in which the first vision was given
• Sabath is interpreted “rod”, and signifies the harsh correction by which the people was still weighed down.
**“of the eleventh month”** — Eleven is unclean, and belongs to the union of the flesh. Rightly, then, what follows is seen by the Jewish people in this month: for as February is the sharpest in the cold of winter, and as the twenty-fourth day of the month, the moon waning, has a night darker in its shadows, so the people to whom these things were announced was for the most part in exile among the Medes and Chaldeans and Assyrians, weighed down as it were by the blind and lasting horror of night and cold.
**“in the second year of Darius”** — again
**“the word of the Lord came to Zacharias the son of Barachias, the son”** — otherwise: of the son
1.8:
**“I saw by night”**
• Before the people of God was led into captivity and Jerusalem destroyed, Moses saw face to face, and Isaias saw “the Lord sitting upon a throne high and elevated”; but this vision, given to a people set under heavy servitude, is said to have been made by night.
• Allegorically. By the night in which the vision is seen the obscurity of the mysteries is signified. The man upon the red horse is the Saviour, whose garments, that is, his flesh, are red with the blood of the passion; to the captive people he is shown on a red horse, in John’s Apocalypse, the people now set free, he is shown in white. He stands among the myrtle trees, that is, the angelic powers, which ministered to him even in the bottom, that is, when he was set in the flesh; and behind him were horses, red, speckled and white, namely the apostles and apostolic men, who travel through the whole world: some of them red with martyrdom, some speckled with works and teaching and the variety of signs, some white with virginity and soundness of doctrine and purity of heart. When the prophet asked the Saviour to reveal the secrets of the prophetic sense, he promises to show what he sees; and when he has promised, it is not he but the one standing among the myrtle trees who answers: These are the apostles, who are sent by the Lord to fill the whole world with their teaching; who, their office fulfilled, return to the “angel of great counsel” with thanksgiving, saying: We have fulfilled the work enjoined, and the earth, desert before, is inhabited by God and rests from the wars of the vices. That full mercy is asked for refers to this: that neither Jerusalem, that is, the Church, nor the cities of Juda, that is, the souls that confess God, will receive true freedom until, the seventy years of this world being passed, true peace comes and the sabbath rest is fulfilled. Then the Lord answers good and comforting words, namely that “we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away”; and freed from the Babylon of this world we shall cry: “When the Lord brought back the captivity of Sion.”
**“and behold a man”** — The Hebrews think this man is the angel Michael, the avenger of sins in Israel; and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom, namely among the prophets and saints who were in the depth of the people’s captivity. This man was followed by horses, red, speckled and white. Some, changing the order, take the white for the Persians and Medes, under whom the captivity was released and the temple restored; the speckled for the Macedonians, of whom some were friends, others persecutors; the red for the Romans, bloody and cruel, who slew the people and overthrew the temple. Others, following the order of the letter, interpret the man who mounts the red horse and the rest who follow as the four kingdoms: the first and second, the bloody ones, the Assyrians and Chaldeans, of whom the first led the ten tribes captive under Salmanasar, the second Juda and Benjamin, when Jerusalem was burned and the temple overthrown; the third and fourth, the speckled and white, the Medes and Persians, of whom some were merciful, as Cyrus, and Darius son of Hystaspes, and Assuerus, whom the Greeks call Artaxerxes; others cruel, as Cambyses and the rest.
1.9: **“And I said: What are these, my Lord?”** — not knowing what I had seen, I wished to know the meaning of my vision
1.10:
**“And the man that stood among the myrtle trees answered, and said”** — the angel who spoke with me keeping silent
**“These are they, whom the Lord hath sent to walk through the earth”** — These are the kingdoms which the Lord commanded to bring the earth under their power
1.11:
**“And they answered”** — the angels who were set over kingdoms and nations
**“the angel of the Lord, that stood among the myrtle trees, and said: We have walked through the earth, and behold all the earth is inhabited”** — full of men
**“behold all the earth”** — All kingdoms under us are safe and at peace, nor are any pressed by distress. From their answer the angel who intercedes for Israel takes the occasion to pray for the people, and says: Since the whole world is quiet and at peace, why, O Lord, dost thou not have mercy on Jerusalem, especially since, according to thy promises, the time of the captivity is fulfilled?
1.13:
**“And the Lord answered the angel, that spoke in me, good words”** — about the promise of things to come
**“comfortable words”** — about the need of the present
1.14:
**“And the angel that spoke in me, said to me: Cry thou, saying”** — Cry, saying. Behold the good and comfortable words which the prophet is commanded to cry.
**“I am zealous for Jerusalem”**
• When Jerusalem fell away from my love, I, like a bridegroom who loves chastity, wished to call her back by measured scourges to the chastity of my love; had I not loved, I would not have been jealous. Whence, on the contrary, it is said through Ezechiel to her who wholly despised her husband: “I will be angry no more with thee, and my jealousy shall depart from thee.”
• Jerusalem is “vision of peace”, Sion “watching” or “watchtower”. This is she who desires not the wars of the world, nor human and earthly things, but the peace and concord of the saints and the heights of heaven. Being angry with her daily for her vices and her cooling charity, the Lord hands her over to persecutors. But the adversaries, fulfilling their own cruelty, not God’s will, fill her with the blood of the slain from gate to gate. But the Lord in mercy promises that he will rebuild her, and that the plumb line, or measuring cord, is to be stretched in her according to the measure and rank of each. The temple is the Lord’s body, which the ungodly destroyed by the passion, but which was raised in the resurrection; which was the seedbed and the beginning of all the houses of which the Apostle speaks: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwelleth in you.”
1.15: **“with the … nations”** — These are the horses he named above, the red, white and speckled, to whom he handed the Jews over for correction, as a son to a tutor. But those nations, not knowing God’s counsel, punished them as enemies, and raged against those handed over to them.
1.16:
**“Therefore thus saith the Lord”** — because the adversaries crushed them more than I had wished, more than my jealousy intended, therefore I will return
**“I will return to Jerusalem in mercies”** — not in one mercy but in many
**“my house”** — that is, the temple
**“shall be built in it”** — under Zorobabel and Jesus son of Josedec
**“saith the Lord of hosts: and the building line”** — the masons’
1.17:
**“Cry yet, saying”** — not with straining of the voice but of the mind
**“Cry yet”** — The angel who had said to the prophet, Cry, urges him to cry yet again.
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts: My cities shall yet flow with good things: and the Lord will yet comfort Sion”** — the cities you see laid waste by the fire of Babylon will abound again with all good things, and God will comfort their past misery with present good things
**“My cities”** — Allegorically. The cities are the churches, or the souls of the saints, to whom belong the true good things. Whence: “I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.” With these good things, after the fires of persecution which the churches suffered from Gentiles or heretics, when peace is restored they flow in a multitude of virtues; and those that had been cast off for their guilt, now built up in virtues, have comfort in the hope of eternal things.
**“and he will yet choose Jerusalem”** — whom a little before he had cast away
1.18:
**“and behold four horns”** — It is the custom of the Scriptures to signify kingdoms by horns. These four horns are understood as the kingdoms of four nations: one of the Babylonians, which had already passed when this vision was seen; the second of the Medes and Persians, which was then standing; the third of the Greeks and Macedonians; the fourth of the Romans. These horns tossed and scattered Juda. The four smiths are understood as angels, who, obeying God, rebuild what the nations had scattered.
**“And I lifted up my eyes, and saw: and behold four horns”** — Allegorically. By the four horns that reign against the people of God the four passions and disturbances of the mind are signified. Whence: “Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice.” Against these the four smiths, as good physicians, are not seen by the prophet, for he could not see them by himself, but are shown by God: namely the four virtues, prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance. These virtues build up whatever the vices destroy. The saints too, who possess these remedies and restore the Church, are called smiths. Whence the Apostle: “As a wise architect, I have laid the foundation.” Or the four smiths are the evangelists, who restore to their former seat Israel oppressed, that is, the mind that sees God, and Juda, that is, the one that confesses God, and Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace; and those whom the nations of the vices had scattered they draw back to salvation.
1.19: **“And I said to the angel that spoke to me: What are these? And he said to me: These are the horns that have scattered Juda, and Israel, and Jerusalem”** — not all at once, but succeeding one another
1.20:
**“And the Lord shewed me”** — I did not see them myself
**“four smiths”** — destroyers of evils, builders of good things
1.21:
**“And I said: What come these to do? and he spoke, saying: These are the”** — indeed
**“horns which have scattered Juda every man apart, and none of them”** — so much that none
**“lifted up his head”** — weighed down by so great a weight of evils
**“and these are come”** — namely these smiths
**“to fray them”** — the kingdoms
**“to cast down the horns of the nations”** — that they may subject them to God
**“that have lifted up the horn upon the land of Juda”** — upon the people of God

2.1:
**“And I lifted up my eyes”** — Some think this was partly fulfilled under Zorobabel and the other leaders who ruled the people of Israel until the coming of the Saviour. The Jews interpret it as the fable of a thousand years, fleshly men seeking fleshly things. Heretics suppose that the heavenly Jerusalem, which had suffered the fall of sinful souls, is to be restored from them. But by Jerusalem the Church is better understood, which is built in the passion and resurrection of Christ, and daily, by him who knows the measures and deserts of each.
**“And I lifted up my eyes, and saw”**
• He who earlier lifted up his eyes and saw sad things in the four horns now lifts up his eyes again to see the man whose name is the Orient, of whom it was said above: “Behold a man riding upon a red horse.” He builds the city whose builder and maker is God.
• This can be taken morally of the souls of believers, which are built daily by the Lord and see his peace.
• Allegorically. Jerusalem is the Church, of which “glorious things are said”, in which “great is the Lord, and exceedingly to be praised”. She is inhabited by men, that is, the people of the law turned to the faith, and by beasts, that is, the Gentiles turned from idolatry to the faith. Or by men are understood the rational and those learned in the Scriptures, by beasts the simple. For these Christ is a wall, a fire round about, so that those dwelling in the midst who were once lukewarm may be warmed, and the adversaries burned up by him.
**“and behold a man”** — Christ
**“in his hand”** — in working and in power
**“with a measuring line”** — a measure dividing to each as he will
2.2:
**“And I said: Whither goest thou? and he said to me: To measure Jerusalem, and to see”** — I will make it appear
**“how great is the breadth thereof”** — charity, which stretches as far as the love of enemies
**“and how great the length thereof”** — perseverance to the end
2.3:
**“And behold the angel that spoke in me went forth, and another angel went out to meet him”** — who spoke to Michael, that he might speak to the prophet
**“And behold the angel”** — The Hebrews think this is Michael; the other who met him, Gabriel, who speaks to Michael that he may tell the prophet what abundance of all things, what multitude of men and beasts, and what strength of walls Jerusalem shall have, which at present is destroyed to embers and ashes. The Jews tell the fable that all these things will come to pass according to the letter: that because of the multitude of men and beasts Jerusalem cannot have a wall, but its wall will be the Lord’s defence, and it will enjoy the glory of him who dwells in its midst.
2.4: **“And he said to him: Run, speak to this young man, saying”** — Compared with the angels, all human nature or knowledge is called childhood, for the angels do not advance into us, but we advance into the angels.
2.6:
**“O, O”** — the threefold call is an urgent warning to flee
**“O, O flee ye”** — In relation to the position of Jerusalem, the Assyrians and Babylonians, who laid waste the people of God, dwelt in the land of the north. The angel who spoke to the angel prophesying in Zacharias now speaks to those who dwelt in Babylon, that from the four winds into which they had been scattered over the whole world they should return to Sion. And: O Sion, who now dwellest in Babylon, return to thy former seat.
**“flee ye out of the land of the north, saith the Lord”** — The north is the coldest wind, which makes hard the hearts it blows on. Those who had gone to the cold of the north, and had been scattered over the whole world, and were living in the night of this world, are commanded to flee to the Church, and, leaving lowly things, to stand in the loftiness of the doctrines.
2.8:
**“After the glory”** — The voice of the Saviour sent by the Father is brought in: having taken flesh, after the glory of the divine majesty he is sent to the nations that robbed the people of God, so that those who before had plundered them may be a prey to those who served them; and the crowd of servants will know that God almighty sent him.
**“he that toucheth you”** — Touching is taken for harassing: so whoever touches the saints of God is as if he wished to harass the apple of his eye, to rob it of clear light. Whence in the gospel: “You are the light of the world.”
2.9:
**“For behold I lift up my hand upon them, and they shall be a prey to those that served them: and”** — so
**“For behold I lift up”** — God lifts up his hand to strike the hostile nations and to lead his people back to Jerusalem, or into the Church; and now by the nations are understood the opposing powers, which daily bring sinners under their power.
**“you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me”** — “He that sent me is with me.”
2.10:
**“Sing praise”** — therefore
**“and rejoice, O daughter of Sion”**
• the Church
• Still the words of the Lord, urging the people, restored after the captivity to its former seat, to rejoice and praise God dwelling in its midst, in whom the nations are to believe.
**“Sing praise, and rejoice”** — Rightly after the captivity the daughter of Sion is called to joy. Whence it is said: “When the Lord shall have turned away the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad.”
**“for behold I come”** — “I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world.”
**“and I will dwell in the midst of thee: saith the Lord”** — “He conversed with men.”
2.11:
**“And many nations shall be joined”** — “Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance.”
**“to the Lord”** — the Father
**“in that day, and”** — then
**“they shall be my”** — as to the Father
**“people”**
• a peculiar people
• this now, because
**“and I will dwell in the midst of thee”** — “I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world.”
**“and thou shalt know”** — from this
**“that the Lord of hosts”** — the Father
**“hath sent”** — into the world
**“me”** — the Son
**“to thee”** — O Church
2.12:
**“And the Lord shall possess Juda his portion”** — those who confess and believe in him
**“in the … land”** — the Church
**“sanctified”** — not elsewhere
**“and he shall … choose”** — from among the wicked
**“yet … Jerusalem”** — those who love peace
**“Jerusalem”** — Whom he had left to temptation in the persecutions of the Jews. Others think these things were fulfilled under Zorobabel and Jesus, when the two tribes, which are called Juda, returned from the captivity of Babylon, the ten being kept in perpetual exile.
2.13:
**“Let all flesh be silent at the presence of the Lord: for he is risen up out of his holy habitation”** — since the Lord is to possess Judea and choose Jerusalem, let every kind of men fear the coming of the Lord
**“for he is risen up”** — God is said to rise when, as it were waking from sleep, he rouses himself to avenge his people; and this out of his habitation, that is, the patriarchs and prophets and apostles, in whom and with whom the Lord testifies that he will come to judgement and to vengeance.

3.1:
**“And the Lord shewed me … the high priest”** — praying for the people’s return
**“And the Lord shewed me”** — The restoration of Jerusalem having been prophesied, whose minister was Jesus the priest, and for which he himself besought God, the devil is brought in as adversary, wishing to keep the people in captivity, but he could not prevail.
**“Jesus”**
• the son of Josedec, who with Zorobabel was set over the people
• The Lord Jesus Christ “is a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech”. Because he cannot be seen in himself, he is shown by the Lord to the prophet through the taking of flesh, standing before the angel, by whom the “angel of great counsel” is understood; not that we perceive two persons in the Son, but that one and the same is shown as a man in filthy garments and is said to appear as an angel, “the mediator of God and men”. He stands who abides with a firm step. And Satan stood on his right hand to be his adversary, because the Lord “was tempted in all things, without sin”; and the tempter stands on the right, because he strives to oppose Christ’s virtues. The Lord rebuke thee: the Lord the Father; not that he who speaks cannot rebuke, but because, from the unity of nature, when the one has rebuked, he who speaks rebukes too, for the Father and the Son are one Lord. Whence: “He that seeth me seeth the Father also.” He chooses the Church, which contemplates the peace of God. He is the brand plucked out of the fire, because he was in the world and was not touched by its burning: “the bush was on fire and was not burnt.” He is also clothed with filthy garments, because “him that knew no sin, for us he hath made sin”. But this filthy garment was taken from him when he blotted out our sins, so that, because he was clothed with filthy garments, we, rising again in him, may always have white garments. The change of garments is his flesh, now immortal and impassible. The mitre upon his head is the splendour of the divine majesty, that the same may be understood as man and God.
**“standing before the angel of the Lord”** — who himself also laboured for the people’s return
**“and Satan”** — the adversary, the devil
**“stood on his right hand”**
• not on the left, because his accusation was true
• We read in Esdras and in Malachias that Jesus with the rest took a foreign wife. So he is truly accused.
• Since, then, Jerusalem has now been chosen out of all the cities of Judea, God not imputing to her the sins she committed, why do you try to overwhelm Jesus, who has escaped from Babylon like a half-burnt brand?
**“Satan stood on his right hand”** — Allegorically, because he snatched from him that people which was once beloved by him. The Gentiles, who had been counted as the left, believed; and the Jewish people, which was counted as the right, turned aside to faithlessness. But because a remnant will be saved at the end, the Lord removes Satan from his right hand, saying: The Lord rebuke thee, O Satan; and he points to the deliverance of the same people, he who chose Jerusalem. This is the brand plucked out of the fire, that is, delivered from the burning of the eternal fire, into which it was sliding under the leading of faithlessness.
**“to be his adversary”** — as if saying he was unworthy to be heard
3.2:
**“And the Lord said to Satan”** — the accuser
**“The Lord rebuke thee, O Satan”** — may God’s rebuke take away the effect of your evil will
**“and the Lord … rebuke thee”** — God speaks of himself in the third person
3.3: **“And Jesus was clothed with filthy garments”** — either for his unlawful marriage, or for the sins of the people, or for the squalor of the captivity
3.4:
**“Who answered, and said”** — commanding in the person of the Lord
**“to them”** — to the other angels
**“that stood before him, saying: Take away the filthy garments from him”** — of which he spoke above
**“And he said to him”** — when they had fulfilled the command in deed, the same angel said to him
**“Behold I have taken away thy iniquity”** — these are the filthy garments
**“and have clothed thee with change of garments”** — I have joined you to an Israelite wife
3.5:
**“And he said: Put a clean mitre upon his head”** — that is, the mitre, by which the dignity of the priesthood is understood, because, the filth of sins being taken away, he now has a clean priesthood
**“and they put a clean mitre upon his head, and clothed him”** — the son of Josedec
3.6:
**“And the angel of the Lord protested to Jesus”**
• the son of Josedec
• Christ
3.7:
**“Thus saith”** — in me
**“the Lord of hosts: If … in my ways”**
• “Behold thou art made whole: sin no more, lest some worse thing happen to thee.”
• Allegorically. The word is directed to Christ, made poor for us in the flesh, to whom, as to the head, is referred whatever is said of his members, and our progress is his victory. So when we have come “unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fulness of Christ”, he will judge the house of God, that is, us who are the Church, setting up in the churches, according to the deserts of each, prophets, apostles, teachers and the like. Whence: “God hath stood in the congregation of gods: and being in the midst of them he judgeth gods”, dividing to each as he will. And then angels will be given him to minister, that is, men who, set in the flesh, will lead the angelic life, who will not waver, but will stand by him in the Church, steadfast with Jesus who stands.
**“If … in my ways”** — After the filthy garment has been washed away and the dignity of a clean priesthood restored, Jesus son of Josedec is commanded to keep the ways of God, and the reward is set before him: that therefore he will continue as judge and high priest in the temple of God, and will have some of the number of the angels who stood there at that time, by whose help he would be surrounded against his enemies.
**“thou wilt walk”** — if thy members walk
**“and keep my charge”** — my commandments, which are to be kept
**“thou also”** — in the perfect: this is your reward
**“shalt judge”** — as high priest
**“my house, and shalt keep my courts”** — whence: “Adore ye the Lord in his holy court.”
**“and I will give thee … to walk with thee”** — with thee, who guard thee, by whose help thou mayest not fear thy enemies, being safe
**“some of them”** — angels or saints
**“that are now present here”** — in thy sight
3.8:
**“Hear, O Jesus thou high priest”** — He had promised Jesus son of Josedec that he would judge his house, and keep his courts, and have angels as ministers of angelic dignity; now he says to him and to his friends, that is, his disciples and the prophets, who are portending men, that is, set as a sign of things to come, that they shall have full happiness and clear-sighted blessedness when he comes “whose name is the Orient”. He is also called the corner stone, joining two walls into one, upon whom are seven eyes, of which Isaias says: “And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and of understanding, the spirit of counsel and of fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and of godliness. And he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord.”
**“Hear, O Jesus thou high priest, thou and thy friends that dwell before thee, for they are portending men: for behold I WILL BRING MY SERVANT THE ORIENT”** — Allegorically. Jesus the high priest is the Lord, the Saviour; his friends the apostles, who are portending men, that is, taking or seeing his deeds mystically, and knowing the future from the present, as those who interpret the man born blind as the people of the Gentiles. He is also, by another figure, called the Orient, for his light, and the stone which according to Daniel was cut out of the mountain, for his strength, by which he breaks in pieces all kingdoms. So it is said to Christ: thou and thy apostles, hear the promises which I have made to be fulfilled in you; and at once the word turns to the hearers, speaking of Christ himself: For behold I will bring my servant, the Lord, namely Christ, who is also the stone that breaks the enemies. Whom I have laid before Jesus son of Josedec, because he came after him, and was given before his face, for he understood that he himself prefigured him; in whom alone are seven eyes, because in him was the fulness of all spiritual grace.
3.9:
**“For behold the stone”** — is brought
**“that I have laid before Jesus: upon one stone”** — this
**“there are seven eyes: behold I will grave the graving thereof, saith the Lord of hosts: and I will take away the iniquity of that land in one day”**
• He keeps the metaphor of the stone, as if to say: I will have this stone wounded by the nails of the cross and the soldier’s lance, and in his passion the iniquity of the land will be blotted out, in one day, of which it is said: “This is the day which the Lord hath made: let us be glad and rejoice therein.” And on that day of the passion a man, that is, the man perfect in Christ, will call his friend, that is, those who believe from among the Jews or the Gentiles, to be under the vine, whose fruit “maketh glad the heart of man”, and who said, I am the vine; and under the fig tree, that is, the sweetest refreshment of the Holy Spirit.
• The Septuagint: Behold I will dig a pit. The Jews refer this to the end of the world, when Christ will come to judge, who will dig, that is, bring into the open the works of each; and on that day each of the saints will call his friend, that is, the other saints, to rest, that they may rejoice in the virtue of their works.

4.1:
**“And the angel that spoke in me came again: and he waked me, as a man that is wakened out of his sleep”**
• of rest, or of ignorance
• He who sleeps with that sleep of which it is said, “If he sleep, he shall do well”, can sing with the bride: “I sleep, and my heart watcheth.”
• The angel questions him when he is awakened so that, when he answers that he does not know, we may learn from the angel.
**“And the angel … came again”** — He who spoke in the prophet is nowhere seen to have gone away; but we must know that whenever human frailty is left to its own weakness, God and the help of his angels go away from us. So the prophet too, struck by the amazement of the great vision, was dull in his whole mind, and could not see the clear light of the truth. Hence, to see another vision, he is roused as if from sleep.
4.2:
**“And he said to me: What seest thou? And I said: I have looked, and behold a candlestick all of gold, and its lamp upon the top of it”**
• of the candlestick
• Allegorically. The candlestick is the Church, golden for its spiritual understanding of the Scriptures. The lamp is Christ, who shines in the Church. The seven lights and the funnels are the graces of the Holy Spirit, through which the Church receives the oil of God’s mercy. The two olive trees are Moses and Elias, that is, the law and the prophecies, which proclaimed Christ’s passion; or the olive trees are the gospel, which is on the right, and the law, which is on the left. The mountain is the devil and Antichrist, who dares to raise himself against Christ, who said to Zorobabel: “All these will I give thee, if falling down thou wilt adore me”; whom the Lord treads down, saying: “Begone, Satan: for it is written: The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve.” The chief stone is “the Word that was in the beginning with” the Father, which is brought out of “the bosom of the Father” in the flesh; who makes the grace of the law equal to the grace of the gospel, so that both the believers from Israel and the people of the Gentiles may receive an equal gift.
**“and behold a candlestick”** — The Hebrew says that by the golden candlestick the law is signified; by the lamp on its top, Christ, who is the head of the law and gives light to the world; by the seven lights, the seven lamps of the Holy Spirit, which are fully in Christ, and which are upon the candlestick because the law was written at the Holy Spirit’s dictation; by the seven funnels, through which oil is poured into the lights so that they may shine on the candlestick, it is understood that through the law seven graces come down from heaven to men. By the two olive trees on the right and left, between which the lamp shines in the middle, he interprets the law and the prophets. The angel whom the prophet asks he understands as the mind enlightened by God, which shows us God’s will; which does not answer but asks, not from ignorance, but to rouse him to understanding. Not with an army, nor by might: the word of the Lord to Zorobabel is itself the interpretation of the vision, about the bringing back of the people, which will not be done by a multitude of warriors; but the people was brought back by God’s spirit, and the adversaries laid waste. By the great mountain that stands before Zorobabel the devil is interpreted, who opposes Jesus and is lifted up against Zorobabel and the people of the Jews; but he is seen as a plain, because he is laid low and humbled under the feet of Israel; and in spite of him God brings out the chief stone, that is, Christ his Son, who was always the help of the people of Israel; and by the grace of that stone he made equal, in those he brought back from captivity, the grace he had shown to their fathers.
**“and the seven lights thereof”** — of the lamp
**“upon it”** — the candlestick
**“and seven funnels”** — there were
**“for the lights”** — through which oil is poured into the lights
4.3:
**“And two olive trees”** — there were
**“over it: one upon the right side of the lamp”** — the gospel
**“and the other upon the left side”** — the law
**“thereof”** — of the lamp
4.6:
**“And he answered, and spoke to me, saying: This is the word of the Lord to Zorobabel”** — this is the interpretation of the vision, which God reveals
**“saying”** — this
**“Not with an army”** — that is, in a multitude
**“nor by might”** — of warriors
**“but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts”**
• the bringing back of the people is done, and the laying waste of the enemies
• but
4.7:
**“Who art thou”** — art
**“O great mountain, before Zorobabel? thou shalt become a plain”** — thrown down from on high
**“and he shall bring out”** — the Lord
**“the chief stone”** — Christ, who is “the firstborn of the dead”
4.9:
**“The hands of Zorobabel”** — The princes of those returning had laid the foundation of the temple and finished it; and when you see the top set on the temple you are now building, you who now doubt will then know that I, Zacharias, announced whatever I said by God’s inspiration.
**“The hands of Zorobabel have laid the foundations of this house”** — Allegorically. Zorobabel is Christ, who founds and perfects the Church; in whose hand is his body, not of lead, but of tin, most pure from all sin. The seven eyes that run through the whole earth are the seven spirits, for nothing is hidden from the Lord, but he knows the past and the future and the present, “and will render to every man according to his works”.
**“and his hands shall finish it: and you shall know”** — then
**“that the Lord of hosts hath sent me”** — Zacharias
**“to you”** — as if to say: few are they who despise the height of kings; but Zorobabel despised it, and his companions
4.10:
**“For who hath despised little days?”** — a description of human life
**“For who”** — Truly Zorobabel and his companions, trusting in God’s help, will count as nothing the days of the kings who wish to hinder God’s work; for though they see them shining in purple and surrounded by an army, yet they will understand that their life is short and evil and can do nothing against God; and so they will rejoice at the completion of the work, and will see the help of the Saviour, who is promised from the stock of Zorobabel, who is a stone of tin for strength, a strong and sturdy wall. For as tin protects other metals from fire, and though bronze or iron is by nature very hard, yet without tin it is burned and consumed, so all the strength of angels and men, if it has not the Saviour’s help, is weak and frail.
**“and they shall rejoice, and shall see the tin plummet in the hand of Zorobabel”** — and
**“These are the seven eyes of the Lord”** — which you saw in the stone
4.11:
**“And I answered”** — he answering nothing
**“What are these two olive trees”** — Because he did not answer what I had asked, since it was above me and I did not deserve to hear, I asked lesser things, according to that: “Knock, and it shall be opened to you.”
**“and said to him: What are these two olive trees upon the right side of the candlestick, and upon the left side thereof?”**
• The two olive trees had been spoken of above; because the prophet did not keep hold of it, he does not deserve to hear when he asks here; or what was said more obscurely there he wishes to hear more plainly here. Or surely his boldness is refuted by the angel’s silence, because he strives to know things greater than himself. The Hebrews say that because he had not asked all he ought to have known, nothing is answered him here about the olive trees; but he asks more fully, adding the ears, or branches, of the olive trees, about which he had been silent above.
• Allegorically. By the two olive trees, the two testaments: the spiritual gospel on the right, the bodily law on the left; and because we cannot explain the whole gospel nor the whole law, we pick out as it were little branches from them, for “we know in part, and we prophesy in part”. Others interpret the two olive branches, or ears, and the sons of oil, that is, of richness or of splendour, as the priesthood and the law, which give joy to the whole earth. Others as Enoch and Elias, of whom one pleased God in uncircumcision, the other in circumcision, and who were caught up into heaven with the body.
4.12:
**“And I answered again”** — he answering nothing
**“and said to him: What are the two … branches”**
• or branches
• by a metaphor, because the trees stood straight like ears of corn; and as the ear is fenced with its beards, so these, hedged with branches and covered with leaves, rose on high
• he had not asked about the ears above
**“olive … that are by the two golden beaks, in which are the funnels of gold?”** — the Septuagint: the two branches that are in the hands of the two nostrils

5.1:
**“And I turned”**
• to another vision, from glad things to sad
• Above he had seen the building of the temple and the coming of Christ, and had announced the people set free from Babylon; but lest he be lifted up by the happiness he had seen, he sees sad things too, so that he may be humbled by the threat of sad things.
**“and lifted up my eyes: and I saw, and behold a volume flying”** — the Septuagint: a flying sickle, that is, God’s judicial sentence, which cuts down the offences of all
**“a volume flying”** — In which the sins of all are written, so that each may receive according to his sins, whether good or evil. Whence it is said: “The books were opened.”
5.2:
**“I see a volume”** — GREGORY. What is the flying volume but holy Scripture, which, while it speaks of heavenly things, raises the aim of our mind to higher things? For while we see it above us, we avoid attending to, that is, coveting, vain things. It is said to have a breadth of ten cubits and a length of twenty, because the breadth of our working is single, and the long patience of hope is stretched to double: when for a good work both rest of mind is prepared for us here and eternal joys there, as the Truth testifies, saying: “Every one that hath left house, or lands, and so on, shall receive an hundredfold in this world, and shall possess life everlasting in the world to come.” The number a hundred is made perfect by ten multiplied by ten; so he receives a hundredfold who, though he has nothing, yet by the very perfection of his mind seeks to have nothing already in this world. Because, then, by this the double is returned to us for the single, rightly this volume, which is ten wide, stretches twenty cubits in length. But because these same holy words are unto eternal damnation for those who either will not know them, or, knowing them, despise them, rightly it is said of this volume: This is the curse that goeth forth over the face of the earth. And why it is cursed he adds: for every thief, as is there written, shall be judged.
**“And he said to me: What seest thou? And I said: I see a volume flying: the length thereof is twenty cubits, and the breadth thereof ten cubits”**
• Some say that twenty and ten, which are thirty, refer to the age of Christ, for “the Father doth not judge any man, but hath given all judgment to the Son”.
• In twenty, which is made of two tens, harsh and sad things are announced; in ten, that is, one ten, better and prosperous things. So in all these numbers sad things are spoken first and glad ones afterwards, because God chastises in order to amend, and Israel is taught through all the punishments. This is the curse against those who think theft and perjury are small crimes: it is said that the curse written in the volume, or sickle, comes upon the house of the thief and the perjurer, remaining there and laying all waste. What, then, of the crimes reckoned greater, such as “adultery, murder, sacrilege”?
5.3:
**“And he said to me: This is the curse that goeth forth over the face of the earth: for every thief … as is there written”** — in the volume
**“shall be judged”** — shall be condemned
**“and every one that sweareth in like manner shall be judged by it”** — because
5.4:
**“I will bring it forth, saith the Lord of hosts: and it shall come to the house of the thief, and to the house of him that sweareth falsely by my name: and it shall remain”** — a long time
**“in the midst”** — within
**“of his house, and shall consume it, with”** — in like manner
5.5:
**“And the angel went forth”** — The angel who spoke in the prophet went out from him, and, speaking as if he were the Lord, commands him to lift up his eyes and see the heaped-up measure of the sins of many, the offences of all made perfect and filled up. This vessel is the eye, that is, the showing of the sins, so that those whose vices were at first hidden and scattered might be laid open to the eyes of all, heaped together into one. For when Israel goes out of its place into captivity, it is shown to all nations what it was like in its own land. By the mass of lead is signified the most heavy weight of sins; and upon this vessel of all offences sat wickedness in the midst, that is, idolatry, which exceeds all the sins of Israel and gloried in its crime; but it is cast into the midst of Babylon and weighed down by the evil of captivity by God’s angel, so that she who before rejoiced in crime may fall into eternal silence.
**“Lift up thy eyes”** — God, wishing to show the prophet by what fault above all the human race slips away from God, signified by the image of a vessel the open mouth, as it were, of avarice. For avarice is like a vessel, which keeps the mouth of the heart open in its craving. And he said: This is their eye in all the earth. We see many men of dull sense who are yet roused by the goads of avarice in what they crave; and those who are blind to seeing good things become wide awake to carrying them out when rewards spur them on. And behold a talent of lead was carried. What is the talent of lead but this same avarice, the weight of sin? Wickedness is cast into the midst of the vessel, because wickedness is always held in avarice. The mass of lead is put into the woman’s mouth, because the wickedness of avarice is weighed down by the weight of its own sin.
5.6:
**“And I said: What is it? And he said: This is a vessel”** — or: a measure
**“going forth”** — by this vessel I show you the sins of the people
**“And he said: This is their eye”** — the Septuagint: iniquity
**“This is a vessel”** — The vessel, or measure, was carried in the air, and the angel himself gave it a name. This is the eye, that is, the showing of all sins; and behold a woman sitting in the midst of the vessel, or measure, who is wickedness. And as he saw these things, behold a mass of lead like a stone was carried, either by its own force, or by God’s command, or by another whose name is not told. And the angel who spoke in the prophet, going out from him, showed him everything; he cast the woman headlong into the midst of the vessel, she who before was carried freely and, sitting on the vessel, was visible to all; and lest she raise her head again and rejoice in her wickedness, he puts the talent of lead like a stone into the mouth of the vessel, crushing wickedness and shutting it in so that it cannot break out.
5.7: **“And behold a talent of lead was carried, and behold a woman sitting in the midst of the vessel”** — the angel
5.8:
**“This is wickedness. And he cast her into the midst of the vessel, and cast the weight of lead”** — where and by whom it is carried, once shut in, the following passage teaches
**“upon the mouth thereof”** — of the vessel
5.9:
**“and behold there came out two women”** — By the two women the Jews interpret the kingdoms of the Medes and of the Macedonians, both of which afflicted the Babylonian people, and there their wickedness set up its seat. They invent this so that what was said of them may not be understood of them.
**“And I lifted up my eyes and looked: and behold there came out two women, and wind was in their wings, and they had wings like the wings of a kite: and they lifted up the vessel between the earth and the heaven”** — The two women who go out of their land are Juda: the ten tribes that were taken by the Assyrians, and the two that were taken by the Chaldeans. In their wings was wind, that is, the power of the devil; snatched away by the evil spirit as if by wind and breath, they were carried in swift flight. The kite is a most rapacious bird, by which is meant the devil, to whose power Juda and Israel are handed over to be led by him into captivity. And those women carried the vessel, or measure, in which wickedness was held shut, pressed down under the mass of lead, through the air between heaven and earth. The prophet, taught above about the vessel, does not ask what they carry, seeing the vessel borne, but whither they carry it; and the angel answers: That a house may be built for it in the land of Sennaar. Sennaar is the plain of the Chaldeans, where Babylon was built. So these women carry wickedness into Babylon, that a sure house may be built for it there. For truly in Babylon is the sure seat of wickedness.
**“two women”** — GREGORY. What else do we take in these two women but the two chief vices, namely pride and vainglory, which are without any doubt joined to wickedness? And they are said to have wind in their wings, because in their actions they serve the will of Satan. They call him a spirit, of whom it is said in the gospel, when “the spirit is gone out of a man”. And they had wings like the wings of a kite. The kite is always eager to snatch chickens. So these women have wings like the wings of a kite, because their actions are without doubt like the devil, for they always lie in wait to snatch the little ones. And they lifted up the vessel between the earth, and so on. Pride and vainglory have this proper to them, that they lift above the rest the one they have infected in his thinking, and, now by the craving for things, now by the desire for dignities, raise to the height of honour the one they have once caught and hold. But he who is between heaven and earth both forsakes the depths and in no way reaches the heights. These women, namely pride and vainglory, so lift up the captured mind that it forsakes any neighbours as if despising them, and seeks high things, glorying; so it can neither keep brotherly equality with its neighbours nor yet reach the heights. Sennaar is “their stench”: as “a good odour” comes from virtue, so on the contrary stench comes from vice. “For the desire of money is the root of all evils”; and because every evil is begotten through avarice, it is fitting that the house of avarice should be built in stench. Sennaar is a very wide valley, which was called Babylon for the confusion of minds and tongues; and because it is certain that all evils spring up through avarice and wickedness, rightly they are said to dwell in confusion.
5.11:
**“And he said to me: That a house may be built for it in the land of Sennaar”** — a shaking out of teeth
**“and that it may be established, and set there upon its own basis”** — that it may rest there in an everlasting abode

6.1:
**“And I turned”** — I passed to another vision
**“and lifted up”** — higher, to heaven
**“my eyes”** — of the heart
**“and saw: and behold four chariots came out from the midst of two mountains”** — what above he calls myrtle trees, shady, he here calls of brass
**“and the mountains”** — those
**“were mountains”** — which no age can wear away
**“of brass”** — were
6.2:
**“In the first chariot were red horses”** — they were bloody and murderous, and terrible with Babylonian cruelty
**“and in the second chariot black horses”** — the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, which, going forth by king Assuerus’s edict, carried the sad news of the death of all the Jews
6.3:
**“And in the third chariot white horses”** — the Macedonians, under whose king Antiochus we read of the victory of the Machabees
**“and in the fourth chariot grisled horses, and strong ones”** — the Roman kings, of whom some were merciful to the Jews, as Julius Caesar, others persecutors, as Vespasian
6.4: **“And I answered, and said to the angel that spoke in me: What are these, my lord?”** — What do they signify?
6.5:
**“And the angel answered, and said to me: These are the four winds of the heaven, which go forth to stand before the Lord of all the earth”**
• that is, the four quarters of the world, which stand by and obey the Lord; for these four kingdoms did nothing without God’s will
• Some say the four chariots are the four gospels, the horses the apostles: some of them red with martyrdom, some dark and black with the depth and knowledge of the mystery, some white with the grace of virginity, some grisled and strong, having the grace of healings and of various powers. These chariots are sent into the four quarters of the world to fulfil God’s will, and the angel says to them: Go, walk throughout the earth, sow the gospel in all the ends of the earth. Behold, they that go forth into the land of the north: the spirit of the Lord, or of the angels, is said to have rested, when in the land of the north the devil’s most stubborn kingdoms were overthrown by the apostolic preaching.
**“These are the four winds”** — Note that in the holy Scriptures the regions of the world are named according to the position of Jerusalem and the temple.
6.6:
**“That in which were the black horses went forth into the land of the north”** — That in which were the black horses went forth. What the first chariot, with the red horses, did is not said. For when the prophet was relating this, the kingdom of the Babylonians had already passed and the Medes held all Asia, under whose king Darius, in his second year, all the things we have set out above were seen. So the black horses went forth into the land of the north, namely to overthrow the kingdom of the Chaldeans.
**“and the white went forth after them: and the grisled went forth to the land of the south”** — that is, the Romans, strong and sturdy, went forth to the southern quarter and laid waste the whole land with swift onslaught
**“and the grisled went forth”** — The kings of the Macedonians follow in the footsteps of the Medes; and as the Medes subdued the Chaldeans, so the Macedonians subdued the Medes and Persians and Chaldeans.
6.7:
**“And they that were most strong, went out, and sought to go, and to run to and fro”** — otherwise: to run to and fro
**“through all the earth. And he said: Go”** — the angel who spoke in me cries to the Roman empire
**“walk throughout the earth: and they walked throughout the earth”** — lay all things under your feet
6.8: **“Behold they that go forth”** — The Hebrews hand down that the white horses, that is, Alexander and the Macedonians, who went forth after the Medes into the land of the north, made the prophetic spirit rest in the land of the north, because they fulfilled God’s will against the Medes, and in a short time the empire of the Medes and Persians was wiped out by the Macedonians. For it is a great comfort to those who are oppressed if they know their enemies will soon perish.
6.10:
**“Take”** — Take the gifts they offer, gold and silver.
**“of them of the captivity”** — from those who returned from the captivity, namely from Holdai and from the others
**“of Holdai”** — entreaty of the Lord
**“and of Tobias, and of Idaias; thou shalt come in that day, and shalt go into the house of Josias, the son of Sophonias, who came out of Babylon”**
• who was keeper and warden of the temple of the Lord, and there the crowns will rest in an everlasting place
• Holdai: entreaty of the Lord. Tobias: good of the Lord. Idaias: known of the Lord. For Holdai, Helem, that is, a dream, will be set afterwards, and in the fourth place Hem, that is, grace, will be added. The captivity of the Jews, that is, of the people that confesses God, is vices and sins. Those who repent return to Jerusalem, that is, the Church; by these, who entreat God in penance and are well pleasing to God, and known, that is, approved, by God, gold and silver are offered, of which crowns are made in the house of Josias, who is called “saved”, and is the son of Sophonias, that is, of the visitation of the Lord, because he who had been sick before is visited by the Lord and saved. These crowns are set on Jesus, that is, Christ, who is crowned in his members as they return; who is the son of Josedec, which is interpreted “Lord of justice”, because Christ “renders to every man according to his works”. To him it is said: Behold a man, the Orient is his name. We do not divide Jesus, nor make two persons of one; but he who is called Jesus because he saves is himself the Orient, because in his days justice arose. Under this Orient a multitude of believers will spring up, which will build the Church for God; and he, crowned in each of his members, will bear their glory; and he, king and high priest, will sit on a throne both royal and priestly, and “the counsel of peace shall be between them both”, because both glories will agree in the Lord Jesus. After Christ is crowned, a crown is promised also to those who dream of him, “through a glass in a dark manner”, and to whom the Lord is good, and who are known by God and, filled with his grace, are visited by him; and those who once groaned in Babylon, far from Judea, will build the house of God by their several advances, and all with one mind will know that God sent the prophet to them.
6.11:
**“And thou shalt take gold and silver: and shalt make”** — in the house of Josias
**“crowns”** — not one but two, distinguished by the difference of gold and silver
**“and thou shalt set them”** — one of them
6.12:
**“And thou shalt speak to him, saying: Thus saith the Lord of hosts, saying: BEHOLD A MAN, THE ORIENT IS HIS NAME”** — that is, Zorobabel, who is called the Orient because from a lowly captive he will rise to be leader of the people
**“and under him shall he spring up”** — a multitude of the faithful
6.13:
**“and he”** — after the temple is built
**“shall bear the glory”** — the other crown
**“and shall sit, and rule”** — with the power of a prince
**“upon his throne: and he shall be a priest upon his throne”** — but Jesus son of Josedec too will sit upon the priestly seat
**“and the counsel of peace”** — with minds and counsels joined they will govern the people of God
**“shall be between them both”** — who came down from the royal and from the levitical tribe
6.14:
**“And the crowns shall be to Helem”**
• otherwise: Heleti
• Helem is put for Holdai
• The crowns, first set on the heads of the two, will be consecrated in God’s temple with the names of those by whom they were offered, for an everlasting memorial; and then nations from the whole world that are set far off will come and build in the temple of the Lord, each according to his strength.
**“the crowns shall be”** — The Hebrews say that Ananias, Azarias and Misael, returning from captivity, brought gold and silver as gifts for the temple, and crowns for the high priest and the leader; and that Hem, whom he had not named above, that is, “grace”, namely Daniel, came with a gift; and that Helem is put for Holdai so that by the meaning of the name, which is “dream”, it may be shown that Daniel, set in captivity, and the three children knew the mysteries of the king’s dream. For Daniel himself and the three children prayed to the Lord, and so Daniel obtained the interpretation of the dream.
**“and Tobias, and Idaias”** — known of the Lord
**“and to Hem”**
• grace
• here a fourth is added, whereas he set only three
**“the son of Sophonias”**
• visitation of the Lord
• and this shall be
**“a memorial”** — for ever
6.15:
**“And they that are far off”** — from God through sins
**“shall come and shall build in the temple of the Lord”** — where God dwells
**“and you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me to you”** — and then from the outcome and prosperity of events you will know that I foretold everything at the Lord’s command
**“But this shall come to pass, if hearing you will hear the voice of the Lord your God”** — all these things will come to pass if you obey the Lord’s commandments

7.1: **“And it came to pass in the … year”** — The Hebrews suppose that Sarasar and Rogommelech and the others who were with them were Persians and captains of king Darius who feared God; who, hearing that the temple had been built, asked through envoys of the priests and prophets whether, according to the former custom, in the fifth month, in which Jerusalem was overthrown by Nabuchodonosor, the reason for fasting and weeping still lasted, now that Jerusalem had been restored, or whether rather, because of the restoration, they should change sorrow into joy; so that the Persians who feared God, as they had wept with the weeping Jews, might rejoice with them as they rejoiced. And after the envoys’ inquiry was finished, the word of God comes to Zacharias, commanding him to tell the people and the priests what they ought to answer the envoys.
7.2: **“When Sarasar, and Rogommelech, and the men that were with him, sent to the house of God, to entreat the face of the Lord”** — that is, to the temple, which had now been restored
7.3:
**“To speak to the priests”** — to inquire of the priests
**“of the house of the Lord of hosts, and to the prophets, saying”** — now that Jerusalem has been restored
**“Must I weep”** — in memory of the destruction
**“in the fifth month”** — which is called July
**“or must I sanctify myself as I have now done for many years?”** — weeping and fasting are called sanctification, because those healed through abstinence are sanctified
7.5:
**“Speak”** — you, the prophet, in my person
**“to all the people of the land”** — which fasts or eats with an earthly affection
**“and to the priests, saying: When you fasted”** — abstained from food
**“and mourned”** — with outward mourning, having lost temporal gladness
**“in the fifth”** — when Jerusalem was taken
**“and the seventh month”** — when Godolias was slain by Ismahel
**“for these seventy years”** — of the desolation of the temple and the overthrow of Jerusalem
**“did you keep a fast unto me?”** — did your fasting profit me at all?
7.6:
**“And when you did eat and drink”** — and on the other hand, if ever you ate or fed
**“did you not eat for yourselves, and drink for yourselves?”** — not for me; for God is not appeased by these things, but by good works, for “meat doth not commend us to God”, but let us do the commandments
7.7:
**“Are not these the words which the Lord spoke by the hand of the former prophets”** — as if to say: I do not change my sentence; what I said while Jerusalem still stood, I say after it is rebuilt
**“Are not these”** — As if to say: why do you ask with such scrupulousness when you ought to fast and mourn, when I have already commanded through Isaias and the other prophets that at all times one must fast from evils and be diligent in works of mercy?
**“when Jerusalem as yet was inhabited, and was wealthy, both itself and the cities round about it, and there were inhabitants towards the south”** — in the hill country
7.9:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts, saying: Judge ye true judgment”**
• lest it be thrown in your face: how long will you judge unjustly?
• These things I wanted more, these I sought, these make a fast commendable; for not doing these you were handed over to captivity. I do not seek the fast of desolation and death of the fifth and seventh months.
**“Judge ye true judgment”** — Moses: “You shall judge the great as the small, and you shall not respect any man’s person, nor have pity on the poor in judgment, because it is the judgment of God.”
**“and shew ye mercy and compassion every man to his brother”** — after the truth of judgement let clemency follow towards all, above all towards brothers, whether of the same blood or of the same faith
7.10:
**“And … the widow, and the fatherless”** — whose care is entrusted to you by God
**“and the stranger, and the poor”** — one is made lowly by wandering, the other by want
**“oppress not … and let not a man … evil … against his brother”** — every man is a brother, for all are from one father
**“devise”** — much less do it
7.11:
**“But they would not hearken”**
• when I had commanded these things, they would not hearken
• These things can be referred to those in the Church who will not hear God, but harden their heart; and so, offending in the Church, they are cast out of the land of confession, and the indignation of God comes upon them, and they are scattered through all the kingdoms of the vices; and their land is made desolate, either the soul or the body, not having God for its dweller nor the spirit returning into it; and the land once delightful, which was the lodging of the Trinity, is turned into a wilderness and a dwelling of dragons.
**“and they turned away the shoulder to depart”** — spurning my commands by the bearing of their body
**“and … ears”** — of the heart
**“their”** — not God’s
**“they stopped”** — with a burden
**“not to hear”**
• God commanding
• “like the deaf asp that stoppeth her ears”
7.12:
**“And they made their heart”** — of their own will
**“as”** — as it were
**“the adamant stone”** — a hard stone
**“as the adamant stone”** — Adamant is a very strong stone, which breaks all metals and is broken by none; whence it is called “untameable”.
**“lest they should hear the law, and the words which the Lord of hosts sent in his spirit by the hand of the former prophets”** — Isaias, Osee, who had clean hands
**“And”** — therefore
**“a great indignation came”** — for great sins
7.13:
**“And it came to pass”** — the words of the Lord were fulfilled, paying like for like: as they walked perversely towards him, so he would walk perversely towards them
**“that as he spoke”** — the Lord, threatening beforehand
**“and they heard not”** — me
**“so shall they cry”** — to me
**“and I will not hear, saith the Lord of hosts”** — them
7.14:
**“And”** — nay rather
**“I dispersed them throughout all kingdoms”** — of the Assyrians, Medes, Chaldeans, Persians and others
**“which they know not: and the land was left desolate”** — all Judea
**“behind them”**
• from their dwellings
• kingdoms
**“so that no man passed through or returned: and they changed the delightful land into a wilderness”** — the land which, compared with others, flowed with milk and honey for its great abundance, they turned into a wilderness

8.1: **“And the word … came”** — The people of Israel committed fornication in captivity with the Assyrians and Chaldeans; but after it was mocked by its lovers and stripped of its former beauty, remembering its former happiness it says: “I will return to my first husband”; and he, taking her back in marriage, says: I have been jealous.
8.2:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts: I have been jealous for Sion with a great jealousy”** — I afflicted the Jews who forsook me and worshipped idols
**“I have been jealous”** — The more I was angered before, because, defiled by many lovers, she stained my bed, the more now am I jealous for her, because she has done penance and built the temple in which I will dwell in her midst.
**“and with a great indignation”** — because their sins were great
**“have I been jealous for her”**
• because, prostituted with many lovers, she stained my bed
• but
8.3:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts”**
• because she repented
• but
**“I am returned to Sion, and I will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem”** — in the temple that has been built
**“and Jerusalem shall be called The city of truth”** — which before was a city of lies
**“and the mountain of the Lord of hosts, The sanctified mountain”** — on which victims are offered and the order of the ceremonies kept
**“I am returned”** — By Sion and Jerusalem are taken the souls of the faithful, watching for God and seeing peace; when they sin God is angry with them, handing them over to captivity, so that they may feel God through evils whom they had not felt through prosperity and good things. And when they have done penance the Lord will return to them, and in those in which the lies of the vices reigned before, Christ, the truth, will dwell, and they will be called the mountain of the house of the Lord.
8.4: **“There shall yet … dwell”** — So great will be the prosperity of all things that, no enemy remaining, both sexes will reach extreme age and hold up their trembling limbs with a staff to guide them. The streets of Jerusalem, that is, of the Church, are the virtues, in which dwell old men, not in age but “whose understanding is grey hairs”. These also have staffs in their hands, that is, correction, saying to their disciples: “What will you? shall I come to you with a rod, or in the spirit of meekness?” And with the old men will dwell old women, of whom Paul says: “Honour widows that are widows indeed.” The city will be filled also with boys and girls playing, whom the psalmist exhorts to sing to the Lord, saying: “Young men and maidens: let the old with the younger praise the name of the Lord.”
8.5:
**“And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls”** — in the peace of cities it is usual for playful youth to celebrate its joys with games and dances
**“playing in the streets thereof”** — showing the gladness of the mind by the bearing of the body
8.6:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts: If it seem hard”**
• by those who see the city utterly destroyed
• and what I promise is as if impossible
• When he had prophesied so great a happiness to the remnant of the people who had come from captivity, it seemed incredible. Against which the prophet says: The answers I give are not mine, nor do I use my own voice; the promises I repeat are God’s.
**“If it seem”** — When, in the time of persecution, the meeting places of the Christians were destroyed, the islands filled with the exiles of the faithful, the divine books burned, who then would have believed that churches would be built by the very men who destroyed them?
**“in the eyes of the remnant of this people”** — faint-hearted
**“in those days”** — when Jerusalem has been built and rejoices
**“shall it be hard in my eyes, saith the Lord of hosts?”** — I who promise with my own mouth, to whom nothing is impossible
8.7:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts: Behold I will save my people from the land of the east”**
• “Many shall come from the east and the west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.”
• We can say these things were fulfilled in part in the time of Zorobabel, when, the people being brought back under the figure of what was to come, God dwelt in Jerusalem. Whence it was called the people of God, and the Lord was called their God, not in falsehood and iniquity, but in truth and justice. And they are fulfilled above all in the Church under Christ, when “many come from the east and the west, and sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven”, and, the shadow of the old law departing, the truth of the gospel and the justice of Christ are made known.
**“Behold I will save”** — Some of the Jews say these things were fulfilled under Zorobabel and Nehemias, when the temple was built and the walls of the city put up, and the state of the Jewish people restored by the Machabees and the various princes who ruled Judea until Herod. Others refer them to the consummation of the world, and say they are to be fulfilled under the Christ for whom they wait in vain.
8.8:
**“And I will bring them”** — “There shall come out of Sion he that shall deliver and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob.”
**“and they shall dwell in the midst of Jerusalem”** — of the Church
**“and they shall be my people”** — obedient
**“and I will be their”** — “There shall be one fold and one shepherd.”
**“God”** — protector
8.9:
**“Thus saith the Lord of hosts: Let your hands be strengthened”**
• for the rest
• It is said to the Church: Let your hands be strengthened by good works, on which the house of God is founded, when the foundations of faith are laid and the temple built, when the multitude of the faithful is strengthened and so lives as to deserve to be God’s temple. But before this building, whatever good work they seemed to have, whether men, that is, the rational, or beasts, that is, the simple, they gained no reward from it with God; but there were wars and discords and tribulation among them; brother supplanted brother, and “a man’s enemies shall be they of his own household”, because they lacked the peace which Christ, going to the Father, left to the apostles. Whatever good work a Jew or a heretic or a Gentile does without faith in Christ, he does without reward; but once faith in Christ is received, those who were held captive in the world for their sins and burned with the Babylonian fire now have the fruit of the vine which says: “I am the true vine.” For them the earth gives its fruit, so that “they that sow in tears shall reap in joy”; and “the heavens, which shew forth the glory of God”, will give the dew of the divine word; and the remnant of the people, which the Lord of Sabaoth has left us, will have all these things, that is, peace and the abundance of the land.
